uploads/science/Resporatory Diseases.doc.searchText: ﻿Chapter 3 Living systems extra worksheet 1: Respiratory diseases Science understanding, Science as a human endeavour Getting oxygen into your body is vital for our survival. Many different diseases of the lungs and respiratory system prevent you from being able to breathe as deeply as normal and breathing may cause you to cough or wheeze. Common diseases of the lungs include asthma, emphysema, bronchitis and pneumonia. These diseases may be chronic, which means they are long lasting or occur over and over again. Other diseases are acute, which means they come on rapidly and last a short time. Asthma Asthma is a chronic disease in which the bronchi in the lungs are swollen and tender. In this condition the bronchi react to factors in the environment, known as triggers. Triggers such as tobacco smoke, dust and pollens cause muscles in the walls of the bronchi to contract, making the airways narrow, as shown in Figure 3.1.1. The cell lining of the bronchi produces extra mucus. The mucus reduces the space inside the bronchi even more and the person has difficulty breathing. When people with asthma feel an attack coming on, they use puffers. The puffer contains chemicals that relax the muscles of the bronchi. This allows the bronchi to open up and the person is able to breathe freely again. Figure 3.1.1 The passage through which air can pass is very narrow during an asthma attack. Emphysema Emphysema is a chronic lung disease in which the bronchi, alveoli and blood capillaries are damaged. Emphysema is usually caused by smoking or long-term exposure to air pollutants (chemicals) and dust. The tissues of healthy bronchi and alveoli are elastic, which means that they are able to stretch and then return to their original shape. When bronchi and alveoli are exposed to pollutants and dust over long periods of time, they lose their ability to stretch. The bronchi become narrow and the alveoli break. Damage to the alveoli creates larger spaces within the lungs. Having large spaces reduces the surface area for gas exchange. The blood capillaries surrounding the alveoli are also damaged and less carbon dioxide and oxygen can be carried to the alveoli and away from them. Compare the photograph of the alveoli of a person with emphysema with the alveoli of a healthy person shown below. Figure 3.1.2 Figure 3.1.3 Alveoli of someone suffering from emphysema Alveoli of a healthy person. People with emphysema become breathless during physical activity and frequently have chest infections. They often have a bluish colour to their skin, especially around their lips. This bluish colour is known as cyanosis and is caused by a lack of oxygen in their blood. Emphysema develops slowly. Damaged alveoli and tissues of the bronchi do not repair themselves so the damage is permanent. A person with advanced emphysema has to breathe hard in an attempt to exhale fully and to get enough air into their lungs. Open your mouth as wide as it can go and then try blowing out a candle or match without making an ‘O’ shape with your lips. It is difficult. This is what breathing is like for people with emphysema, all the time. Questions 1 a Explain the difference between a chronic and an acute disease. b State whether asthma is an acute or chronic disease. Explain your choice 2 Refer to Figure 3.1.2. Propose the effect these holes in the alveoli would have on the person’s breathing. 3 Construct a flow diagram of events from the trigger to an asthma attack. 4 Explain why people with advanced emphysema often have a bluish tinge to their lips. 5 Explain why smoking is not good for the health of your lungs. 6 In many parts of Australia there is a distinct dry season. Explain why the dry season would be a difficult time for people who suffer from asthma. 7 Many coal miners used to suffer from emphysema. Propose why they suffered from it. 8 Compare asthma and emphysema using the table below. Asthma Emphysema Cause Chronic or acute Part of respiratory system affected Treatment

uploads/science/Revising chemical patter.searchText: ﻿Individual Pathways Activity 4.1 Revising chemical patterns 1. Identify the set that contains two metals and a non-metal. (a) Tungsten, niobium, bromine (b) Platinum, boron, neon (c) Fluorine, nitrogen, cobalt (d) Tin, sodium chloride, iodine 2. Identify the correct statement. (a) The number of neutrons in a nucleus always equals the number of protons. (b) When atoms lose electrons they become negatively charged. (c) Calcium atoms become stable when they lose two electrons to form a cation. (d) An anion has an excess of protons over electrons. 3. Select the correct statement. (a) There are two elements in period 2 of the periodic table. (b) The elements of group 2 of the periodic table have two outer shell electrons. (c) Elements of group 2 are more reactive than elements of group 1. (d) Lithium is a member of group 2. 4. Select the correct statement about uranium. (a) Uranium is a synthetic radioactive element. (b) Uranium has more electrons in its shells than Americium. (c) Uranium does not conduct electricity. (d) Uranium is a transition element that belongs to the actinoid series. 5. Select the statement that is true of arsenic. (a) Arsenic is a non-metal. (b) Arsenic is a member of group 4. (c) Arsenic is radioactive. (d) Arsenic is a metalloid. 6. Chlorine and bromine are halogens. Which statement is true? (a) Bromine is a red-brown liquid and chlorine is a yellow-green gas. (b) Both are members of group 7. (c) Both are members of period 3. (d) Chlorine is a non-metal and bromine is a metalloid. 7. Which term best describes the ability of a metal to be bent or rolled into various shapes? (a) Lustrous (b) Ductile (c) Malleable (d) Brittle 8. What is the maximum number of electrons that can exist in the M shell? (a) 8 (b) 18 (c) 32 (d) 50 9. A solution of a copper salt was sprayed into a Bunsen flame. What colour does the flame turn? (a) Green (b) Lilac (c) Yellow (d) Red 10. What is the chemical formula of aluminium oxide? (a) AlO (b) AlO2 (c) Al3O2 (d) Al2O3 11. Bronze is an alloy of: (a) copper and zinc. (b) copper and nickel. (c) copper and tin. (d) tin and brass. 12. The set that contains the metals in decreasing order of activity is: (a) Hg, Pb, Cr, Mn. (b) Hg, Cr, Mn, Pb. (c) Mn, Cr, Pb, Hg. (d) Cr, Mn, Pb, Hg. 13. The name of KHCO3 is: (a) potassium carbonate. (b) potassium hydrogen carbide. (c) sodium hydrogen carbonate. (d) potassium hydrogen carbonate. 14. Answer true or false for each statement. (a) Calcium is an alkaline earth metal. ………….. (b) There are 18 groups in the periodic table. ………….. (c) There are 8 elements in period 1 of the periodic table. ………….. (d) All members of group 1 have one valence electron. ………….. (e) All members of group 18 have eight valence electrons. ………….. 15. Answer true or false for each statement. (a) The modern periodic table is arranged according to atomic number. ………….. (b) The electron configuration of neon is 2,8. ………….. (c) The chemical formula of calcium sulfate is CaSO4. ………….. (d) Carbon monoxide is an ionic compound. ………….. (e) Nickel sulfide is a covalent compound. ………….. 16. Answer true or false for each statement. (a) Silver is more reactive than mercury. ………….. (b) CuFeS2 is a mineral called haematite. ………….. (c) Sulfur trioxide is used to make sulfuric acid. ………….. (d) In a nitrogen molecule, the two nitrogen atoms are linked by a triple covalent bond. ………….. (e) The aqueous solutions of soluble salts conduct electric currents. …………..

uploads/science/revision document for yr.searchText: Curriculum content Questions for revision Recognise that the nervous system enables humans to react to their surroundings and coordinate their behavior Identify the different sections of the nervous system? Central Nervous System and Peripheral Nervous System Give an example of negative feedback? Thermoreceptors detect a decrease in body temperature Muscles shiver, thereby increasing body temperature Give an example of positive feedback? Uterine contractions during labour Secretion of breast milk Recognise the 5 senses What are the five senses? Sight, Hearing, Taste, Smell, Touch Identify the five sense organs? Eyes, Ears, Tongue, Nose, Skin Understand that cells called receptors detect stimuli (changes in the environment) What a re stimuli? Changes in the environment that the body can detect Give examples of stimuli? Light, sound, chemicals, motion, temperature, pain Identify receptors and the stimuli they detect Match the receptor cell to the sense organ? Sense organ Receptor 495300 124460 274320 124460 Eye olfactory nerves 312420 112395 274320 112395 Ear different receptors for each stimuli 495300 131445 Skin tastebuds Tongue rods and cones Nose hairs in the cochlea What categories of receptors are there? Recognise information from receptors passes along cells ( neurones ) in nerves to the brain. There are three types of neurones involved in the nervous system. What are they? Sensory neuron, relay neuron, motor neuron Understand that the brain coordinates the response. What does the CNS compose of? Brain and spinal cord Understand that reflex actions are automatic and rapid. Compare the nervous and endocrine systems? Feature Endocrine system Nervous system Speed of message Slow Fast Speed of response Usually slow Immediate Duration of response Long lasting Short Spread of response Usually slow Very localised How message travels through body In circulatory system — in bloodstream In nervous system — along nerves and across synapses Types of message Hormones (chemicals) Electrical impulse and neurotransmitters (chemicals) Define reflex? An action that involves only a few neurons and travels only to and from the spinal cord. There is no conscious thought (brain not involved) Understand the role of receptors, sensory neurones , motor neurones , relay neurones , synapses and effectors in simple reflex actions. Using the example of someone burning there hand on a hot pan. Explain the process that happens? Draw a reflex arc to show this. STIMULUS (Heat) RECEPTOR ( Thermoreceptors in hand) SENSORY NEURON (sends impuls e to the CNS) RELAY NEURON IN SPINAL CORD (interprets the information and sends impulse to motor neurons) MOTOR NEURON (carries impulse to muscles) EFFECTOR (Muscles in arm contract) RESPONSE (Arm moves away from source of heat) What is a synapse and how does it work? (include the term neurotransmitter) Synapse: A gap between two neurons. When a nervous impulse reaches the end of a neuron, chemicals called neurotransmitters in the first neuron cross the synapse and bind to receptors Map and sketch simple reflex actions Sketch a reflex response model? What part of the body is responsible for regulating temperature? What gland is responsible for regulating water content? What gland is responsible for regulating blood sugar levels? Recognise that the processes within the body are coordinated by chemical substances Processes within the endocrine system are controlled by chemical substances called …………? Name some of these chemical substances and what are there function? Thyroxin Adrenalin Aldosterone Understand that hormones regulate the functions of many organs and cells Link the following hormones to their organ; Testosterone Progesterone Growth hormone Understand that hormones are secreted by glands and are usually transported to their target organs How are hormones secreted by glands transported to their target organs? Label the major glands, the hormones they produce and their target organs Identify examples of types of pathogens such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa and the mode by which pathogens enter the body What is the definition of a pathogen? How can pathogens be transmitted? Give 2 examples of diseases caused by each category of pathogen? (virus, bacteria, fungi, parasites) Define, what is a vector? What is a host? Identify the body’s defence mechanisms such as skin, cilia, tears, mucus, gastric juices, lymphocytes and antibodies First defence line Second defence line Third defence line Explain and give examples of how the different defence lines work? Understand the process of immunisation What is the definition of immunisation? Distinguish between active and passive immunisation? Identify a number of infectious diseases and their symptoms Name three infectious diseases and their symptoms? Identify that some diseases are non-infectious and not caused by pathogens such as genetic diseases and lifestyle diseases Give examples of non-infectious disease and their causes? Identify and discuss how personal choices such as poor diet, lack of exercise, exposure to electromagnetic radiation and high risk factors may contribute to the onset of diseases such as obesity, thrombosis, high blood pressure, heart disease, cancer etc Further Questions: Looking Back page 129 Questions 5 – 9 Looking Back page 174 Questions 1, 3 and 9

uploads/science/revision_atoms_and_ions_.searchText: Atoms and Ions Last minute study sheet Atoms and Ions last minute study sheet Ideas for last minute study sheet 1. 10 questions. Working in pairs. Each student uses the sheet to write 10 questions that could be answered with information on the sheet. The other student could have a different topic sheet. Focus on the students creating specific questions – rather than “what is an atom”, ask “draw a labelled diagram of an atom”. Swap over the question sheets for the other partner to answer (without the sheet). Once finished, use the sheet to check answers. For any answers that are incorrect, use the sheet to correct them. 2. Concept maps. Students use the information on the sheet to create a large concept map. 3. Scaffolded Practice Tests. Create a short test, either paper or online (i.e. Kahoot, FORMS, Education Perfect), where the students are able to use the sheet to help. Repeat the test (or an alternative) the next day, without the information sheet. 4. Expert Groups / Mastermind. Use the sheets to study for a short period of time then hold a class mastermind competition.

uploads/science/Rock Cycle - Revision Gu.searchText: Year 8 Earth and Space Sciences Revision Guide answers Definitions: Rock The solid mineral material forming part of the surface of the earth and other similar planets, exposed on the surface or underlying the soil Mineral Substances that make up rocks each mineral has its own chemical make up. Crystal Geometrically-shaped substance made up of atoms and molecules arranges in one of seven different shapes. The elements that make up a crystal and the conditions present during the crystal’s growth determine the arrangement of atoms and molecules and the shape of the crystals. Igneous rocks Rocks that form from the cooling of lava or magma as it is thrown through the air from a volcanic eruption. Intrusive rock Igneous rock that forms when magma cools below the Earth’s surface. Extrusive rock Igneous rock that forms when lava cools above the Earth’s surface. Sedimentary rock Rocks formed from sediments deposited by water, wind or ice. The sediments are cemented together in layers, under pressure . Erosion A type of weathering in which surface soil and rock are worn away through the action of glaciers, water, and wind Sediments Material broken down by weathering and erosion that is moved by wind or water and collects in layers. Fossils Any remains, impression, or trace of an animal or plant of a former geological age. Layering The action of arranging something in layers Floodplains An area of low-lying ground adjacent to a river, formed mainly of river sediments and subject to flooding. Coal A sedimentary rock formed from dead plants and animals that were buried before rotting completely Metamorphic rocks A rock formed from another rock that has been under great heat and/or pressure Parent rock The original rock from which something else was formed. Rock cycle An idealized cycle of processes undergone by rocks in the earth's crust, involving igneous intrusion, uplift, erosion, transportation, deposition as sedimentary rock, metamorphism, and further melting and igneous intrusion Mineral ore Rocks mined to obtain a metal or other chemical within them Mining Extraction of natural resources from the Earth Environmental impact statement Study of the possible effects of a planned project on the environment Rehabilitation The act of restoring something to its original state, like the rehabilitation of the forest that had once been cleared for use as a mine. Overburden Waste rock removed from below the topsoil. This rock is replaced when the area is restored. Open cut mining Mining that scours out soil and rocks on the surface of the land Underground mining Mining that uses shafts and tunnels to remove rock from deep below the surface Questions: For each of the three different types of rocks, describe their characteristics, how they are formed, and some examples of them. Igneous Sedimentary Metamorphic How it is formed The solidification of magma and lava Weathered grains of rock or biological material. Igneous rock or sedimentary rock which is exposed to great heat and or pressure over time. Examples Basalt, Obsidian, etc Limestone, Shale, etc Marble, Quartzite Does it have layers? No Yes Yes/can be Is it porous? Can be Yes No Level of hardness? Ranges Ranges Hard Does it have grains or crystals? Crystals Grains Both The level of effect of weathering Medium High Low Diagram Write a description for each type of weathering Weathering Chemical Rain water Rainwater is naturally slightly acidic. Minerals in rocks may react with the rainwater, causing the rock to be weathered Acid rain Acid rain is more acidic than rainwater and makes chemical weathering happen more quickly. Biological Animals Burrowing animals such as rabbits can burrow into a crack in a rock, making it bigger and splitting the rock. Plants Plant roots can grow in cracks. As they grow bigger, the roots push open the cracks and make them wider and deeper. Eventually pieces of rock may fall away. Humans Caused by people walking. Over time, paths in the countryside become damaged because of all the boots and shoes wearing them away. Physical Exfoliation When a rock gets hot it expands a little, and when a rock gets cold it contracts a little. If a rock is heated and cooled many times, cracks form and pieces of rock fall away. Wind, rain and waves Wind, rain and waves can all cause weathering. The wind can blow tiny grains of sand against a rock. These wear the rock away and weather it. Rain and waves can also wear away rock over long periods of time. Freeze-thaw process If water gets into a crack in a rock and then freezes , it expands and pushes the crack further apart. When the ice melts later, water can get deeper into the crack. When the rock freezes again, it expands and makes the crack even bigger. This process of freezing and thawing can continue until the crack becomes so big that a piece of rock falls off. What are the similarities and differences between an intrusive rock, and an extrusive rock? Intrusive rocks and extrusive rocks are both igneous in nature. However, intrusive rocks are formed by magma (i.e., below ground) and extrusive rocks are formed by the expulsion of lava (i.e., above ground). Some igneous rocks have pores in them. Are these rocks intrusive or extrusive? Why are there pores in the rock? These rocks are extrusive. The pores in the rock originate from the gases that were present in the lava as it was cooling in the air. What are the major differences between igneous rocks and sedimentary rocks? The biggest difference is that igneous rocks are made up of crystals, whereas sedimentary rocks form by the cementing of grains. Describe the process in which sedimentary rocks are formed. Rock is weathered, resulting in the rock breaking into smaller pieces. A body of water usually carries these pieces along, until the water slows down (like at the mouth of a lake, or the sea). The sediments are then deposited on the bed. Compaction occurs; the weight of sediments on the top start to squash the sediments on the bottom. The water is then squeezed out from the bottom layer, which causes crystals to form. This is called cementation. This process keeps occurring between different layers, and over a lot of time, eventually forming sedimentary rocks. Why is running water an important part of the formation of sedimentary rocks? Water moves the sediments from one point to another, and the point at which water slows down is the area in which sedimentary rock will start to form. What are the two types of materials can form sedimentary rocks? Biological material and mineral grains. How are igneous and sedimentary rocks transformed into metamorphic rocks? Through exposure to large amounts of heat and pressure, over time. What are minerals? Minerals are chemical substances within rocks with a definite chemical composition. What daughter rocks do Limestone and Sandstone form under high heat? Marble and Quartzite What daughter rock does Shale form under high pressure? Slate What are the different types of weathering? Physical, biological and chemical When walking through a park, you notice a large bed of rock has started to crack from it’s underside. A large tree is nearby. What type of weathering is this? Explain how it occurs. This is biological weathering. As the tree has grown over time, the roots have increased in size. This results in pressure building up on the underside of the rock, causing the rock to break over time. A large rock face is situated in an area which, over the course of the year, experiences an average temperature of around -5 degrees in winter, and 30 degrees in summer. Explain why there are deep cracks in the rock face. HINT: What does an average temperature mean? This could be the result of both the changes in the temperature, and freeze-thaw action. An increase in temperature would cause rocks to expand, and to contract on cooling, exacerbating any smaller cracks/spaces in the rock. Freeze-thaw could occur during the winter months when the temperature would range from positive to negative. If any rainfall occurs, this means that water can get into cracks; when the temperature is negative it will freeze, causing the water to expand, making the cracks larger; and then evaporate off. What type of rocks are most susceptible to weathering? Chalk, limestone Explain the difference between weathering and erosion (use definitions and an example). Weathering is the breaking down of rock. Erosion is when the particle are moved away. What are the two main types of mines? Underground, Open-cut What is required for a company to start mining? Environmental impact statement How do mining companies get metal from ore? Chemical processes Draw a labelled diagram of the rock cycle. uploads/science/rock cycle cut out works.searchText: ACTIVITY 24 NAME_____________________ 1. The Rock Cycle Read the information in the textbox below to get some background knowledge about how rocks just keep on changing. The rock cycle describes the geological processes that form rocks. Igneous rocks can change into sedimentary rock or into metamorphic rock. Sedimentary rock can change into metamorphic rock or into igneous rock. Metamorphic rock can change into igneous rock or sedimentary rock. • Let’s start with magma. • When magma cools it forms igneous rock. • On the Earth’s surface, wind and water can break the igneous rock into pieces. This process is called weathering and erosion. These pieces are called sediments. • The sediments can be compacted to make a layer. The layer can be buried under other layers of sediments. After a long time the sediments can be cemented together to make sedimentary rock. • Sedimentary rock can be weathered away to form sediments again. • When sedimentary and igneous rocks are heated they change into metamorphic rock. • Metamorphic rock can also be weathered away to make sediment. • Metamorphic, igneous and sedimentary rock can also be melted back into magma. • The rock cycle never stops. 2. Refer to the ‘Rock Cycle Flowchart’ attached to this sheet. • Working in pairs, carefully cut out the cards. • Next, organise the cards to represent the rock cycle. Keep rechecking the information box and talk about your decisions with your partner. • When you have checked with your teacher, paste them down on a coloured A4 sheet of paper or in your workbook. • Include the heading ‘Rock Cycle Flowchart’ on your A4 sheet or workbook. Adapted from ‘Science Rocks’ by Kathleen Gordon, p. 7-8, 14, 28. (Queensland Resources Council and the Department of Natural Resources and Mines. Minerals Education Victoria Tel: (03) 8614 1851 Fax: (03) 9629 8603 VELS Unit – Treasures from the Earth September 2007 ACTIVITY 24 NAME__________________ Rock Cycle Cards Adapted from “Science Rocks” by Kathleen Gordon, p 7-8, 14, 28 (Queensland Resources Council and the Department of Natural Resources and Mines) Minerals Education Victoria Tel: (03) 8614 1851 Fax: (03) 9629 8603 VELS Unit – Treasures from the Earth September 2007 ACTIVITY 24 Background notes for teachers The Rock Cycle The geological process that forms rocks is cyclical. Each type of sedimentary, igneous or metamorphic rock can be changed into each other type of rock. This is known as the rock cycle. The following explanation starts with igneous rocks. Igneous rocks start as magma. When magma - molten rock under the Earth’s surface – and lava – molten rock on the Earth’s surface – cools and hardens, it forms igneous rock. The igneous rock is broken down over time through the weathering process. These particles of broken rock, or soil, are washed away by water and accumulate in lakes or oceans and harden into rock again – this time as sedimentary rock. As the sedimentary rock is buried under more and more sediments, or comes into contact with magma, the pressure and heat can cause metamorphism to occur. This transforms the sedimentary rock into a metamorphic rock. If metamorphic rock is buried more deeply, temperatures and pressures continue to rise. If the temperature becomes hot enough the metamorphic rock melts and forms the molten rock called magma and so the cycle continues. Adapted from “Science Rocks” by Kathleen Gordon, p 7-8, 14, 28 (Queensland Resources Council and the Department of Natural Resources and Mines) Minerals Education Victoria Tel: (03) 8614 1851 Fax: (03) 9629 8603 VELS Unit – Treasures from the Earth September 2007 ACTIVITY 24 Background notes for teachers Our amazing Earth The Earth The crust of the Earth is made up of rocks and minerals from the tallest mountains to the floor of the deepest ocean. It makes up less than 1% of the Earth’s mass. The continental crust is up to 50km thick while the oceanic crust is, at most, 15 km thick. Most of the rocky crust is covered by either water, sand, soil or ice. The soil is a mixture of small, inorganic particles and organic material (plant and animal remains), which supports the growth of plants such as grass and trees. Most of the crust is made from only eight elements – oxygen, magnesium, aluminium, silicon, calcium, sodium, potassium and iron. These elements along with others are combined to from thousands of rocks and minerals that are very different. The mantle is the solid casing of the Earth and is about 2900km thick making up almost 70% of the Earth’s mass. It consists of silicon, oxygen, aluminium and iron. The core is mainly made up of iron and nickel and makes up about 30% of the Earth’s mass. The liquid outer core is approximately 2200km thick. The solid inner core is about 1220 km thick. Rocks A rock is made up of minerals that have been cemented together, squeezed and heated, or melted and cooled. Rocks are divided into three main groups: • igneous • sedimentary • metamorphic They are classified into these groups because of the way they were formed. Igneous rocks are formed from melted rock that has cooled and solidified. When rocks are buried deep within the Earth, they melt because of the high pressure and temperature. If this molten rock (called magma) cools slowly, usually at depths of thousands of metres, coarse-grained rocks form with large crystals ( for example, granite and gabbro). If the magma cools quickly, usually on the surface after a volcano erupts, the crystals are very small and fine-grained rocks are formed (for example, basalt, rhyolite and obsidian). Some examples of other igneous rocks are: pumice, tuff and andesite. Sedimentary rocks are formed from the cementing together of small pieces of rocks or shells. They are formed at the surface of the Earth, either in water or on land. They are usually made up of many layers of sediments, which include fragments of rocks, minerals and animal or plant material. Sandstone, limestone, shale, gypsum, conglomerate, coal, chert and flint are all sedimentary rocks. Sometimes igneous and sedimentary rocks are subjected to pressures so intense or heat so high they change. They become metamorphic rocks, which form while buried within the Earth’s crust. The process of metamorphism does not melt the rocks, but changes them into denser, more compact rocks. Slate, marble and gneiss are metamorphic rocks. They are transformed from shale, limestone and granite respectively. shale ⇒ slate limestone ⇒ marble granite ⇒ gneiss Adapted from “Science Rocks” by Kathleen Gordon, p 7-8, 14, 28 (Queensland Resources Council and the Department of Natural Resources and Mines) Minerals Education Victoria Tel: (03) 8614 1851 Fax: (03) 9629 8603 VELS Unit – Treasures from the Earth Mar 2007

uploads/science/Rock Cycle Punctuation a.searchText: ﻿ Replace the punctuation in the following paragraphs: The Rock Cycle Rising magma can escape through cracks in the Earth’s crust. It cools and solidifies, creating new igneous rock. This new rock is exposed to the forces of weathering, which break it down into smaller rocks. These are in turn eroded by wind and water, and deposited some distance from its parent rock. Sediments of eroded rock build up over tens of thousands of years and form layers. The lower layers of sediments are compressed and squeezed under increasing pressure to form sedimentary rock. Deep sedimentary layers are subjected to extreme heat and are changed into metamorphic rock, or are thrust up onto the surface to be weathered again. Metamorphic rock can be thrust up onto the surface of the Earth to be weathered, or pushed lower to melt and become magma and start the cycle of rock formation again. This cycle of pressure, heat, cooling and weathering is called the rock cycle. Questions: 1. What type of rock is formed from solidified magma? _________________________ 2. uploads/science/rock cycle worksheet ans.searchText: ﻿Chapter 8 Rocks extra worksheet 3: The rock cycle Science understanding Logical/Mathematical Answers 1 Igneous rocks form by cooling of magma. 2 An igneous rock can become heated again if it contacts magma. The heat melts the rock and then this molten rock can reform into an igneous rock when it cools. 3 Weathering/erosion, compression (compaction) and cementing turn an igneous rock into a sedimentary rock. 4 Heat and pressure turn it into a metamorphic rock. 5 Weathering and erosion (followed by compression and cementing) change metamorphic rocks into sedimentary rocks. 6 Heat and pressure turn sedimentary rocks into metamorphic rocks. 7 If a sedimentary rock meets magma, either by sinking into the crust or meeting magma (and hydrothermal fluids) that is rising into the crust, it can turn into an igneous rock. 8 It summarises the changes that occur to rocks to change them from one type into another. This helps us understand how rocks form and how the crust changes.

uploads/science/Rock Worksheet.doc.searchText: ﻿ Name ______________________ Date ____________ Rock Worksheet Directions: Read the information below carefully and answer the questions that follow on the back side of this paper. Answer the questions as completely as possible. Rocks and Minerals The ground we walk on, build on, and grow gardens on is made of rock. All the rocks in the world are made up of chemicals called minerals. Minerals are solid, inorganic (not living) substances found in and on the earth. Most are chemical compounds, which means that they are made of two or more elements. For example, the mineral sapphire is made up of aluminum and oxygen. A few minerals such as gold, silver and copper are made of a single element. Minerals are considered to be the building blocks of rocks. Rocks can be a combination of as many as six types of minerals. Through a microscope, a rock shows that it is made of crystals of different minerals, all growing together like a puzzle. Three types of rocks make up the Earth’s crust. Rocks are formed in three different ways to produce igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks. Igneous rocks form when molten magma cools and solidifies. Metamorphic rocks form when a rock is chemically changed by heat or pressure to form a new rock type. Sedimentary rocks form when fragments of rocks and other debris are cemented together. Igneous Rocks When a candle burns, a runny wax is formed that trickles down its side and solidifies. Igneous rocks are formed in a similar way. The rocks solidify from a mass of molten rock, such as when a lava flow cools and hardens. Because of the heat needed to form igneous rocks, they are sometimes called “rocks of fire.” There are two main types of igneous rock: extrusive and intrusive. Extrusive types form when molten rock comes to the surface and cools quickly, as with lava. This produces a very fine-grained rock. Intrusive rocks are those that solidified underground, cooling slowly to produce coarse-grained rocks. Examples: Granite, basalt, obsidian. Sedimentary Rocks Sedimentary rocks are formed when sediment (bits of rock plus materials such as shells and sand) get packed together. They can take millions of years to form. You never know what you might find in a sedimentary rock since many rocks of this type are made up of lots of other rocks, or even animal remains, all stuck together. Sedimentary rocks are built up of particles laid down as layers or beds of sediment and are later buried , compressed, and cemented into a solid mass. Most rocks that you see on the ground are sedimentary. Examples: Sandstone, shale, limestone. Metamorphic Rocks Metamorphic rocks are igneous or sedimentary rocks that have been transformed by heat, pressure, or both. Metamorphic rocks are usually formed deep within the Earth, during a process such as mountain building. When you bake bread, you mix flour, yeast, and water together and bake in a hot oven. In a similar way, heat and pressure from the overlying rocks, may change the nature of the rocks below. This process is called metamorphosis, which means “change.” Examples: Schist, slate, marble. Did You Know? Most of the ocean floor is made of basalt. This igneous rock continues to flow from the Earth through an underwater mountain ranges known as “mid-ocean ridges”? Questions - Please write your answers in complete sentences! 1. What is the difference between rocks and minerals? 2. How many types of rocks make up the Earth’s crust? 3. What are the names of the 3 types of rocks? 4. How are igneous rocks formed? 5. What is another name for igneous rocks? 6. What is the difference between to two types of igneous rocks? 7. How are sedimentary rocks made? 8. How are metamorphic rocks made? 9. What does the word “metamorphosis” mean? 10. Which two layers of the Earth are made of rock? 11. What are the names of the other two layers of the Earth, and what are they made of? 12. Write the following layers of the earth in order from most dense to least dense: atmosphere, crust, inner core, mantle, outer core, water.

Because of the heat needed to form igneous rocks, they are sometimes called “rocks of fire.” There are two main types of igneous rock: extrusive and intrusive. Extrusive types form when molten rock comes to the surface and cools quickly, as with lava. This produces a very fine-grained rock. Intrusive rocks are those that solidified underground, cooling slowly to produce coarse-grained rocks. Examples: Granite, basalt, obsidian. Sedimentary Rocks Sedimentary rocks are formed when sediment (bits of rock plus materials such as shells and sand) get packed together. They can take millions of years to form. You never know what you might find in a sedimentary rock since many rocks of this type are made up of lots of other rocks, or even animal remains, all stuck together. Sedimentary rocks are built up of particles laid down as layers or beds of sediment and are later buried , compressed, and cemented into a solid mass. Most rocks that you see on the ground are sedimentary. Examples: Sandstone, shale, limestone. Metamorphic Rocks Metamorphic rocks are igneous or sedimentary rocks that have been transformed by heat, pressure, or both. Metamorphic rocks are usually formed deep within the Earth, during a process such as mountain building. When you bake bread, you mix flour, yeast, and water together and bake in a hot oven. In a similar way, heat and pressure from the overlying rocks, may change the nature of the rocks below. This process is called metamorphosis, which means “change.” Examples: Schist, slate, marble. Did You Know? Most of the ocean floor is made of basalt. This igneous rock continues to flow from the Earth through an underwater mountain ranges known as “mid-ocean ridges”? uploads/science/Rocks cycle and rock typ.searchText: Rocks Rocks and Minerals All the rocks in the world are made up of chemicals called minerals . Minerals are solid, inorganic (not living) substances found in and on the earth . Minerals are the building blocks of rocks. Rocks can be a combination of as many as six types of min erals. Three types of rocks make up the Earth’s crust. Rocks are formed in three different ways to produce igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks. Igneous rocks form when molten magma cools and solidifies. Metamorphic rocks form when a rock is chemically changed by heat or pressure to form a new rock type. Sedimentary rocks form when fragments of rocks and other debris are cemented together. Igneous Rocks The rocks solidify from a mass of molten rock when a lava flow cools and hardens. There are two main types of igneous rock: extrusive and intrusive. Extrusive types form when molten rock comes to the surface and cools quickly, as with lava. This produces a very fine-grained rock. Intrusive rocks are those that solidified underground, cooling slowly to produce coarse-grained rocks. Examples: Granite, basalt, obsidian. Sedimentary Rocks Sedimentary rocks are formed when sediment (bits of rock plus materials such as shells and sand) get packed together . They can take millions of years to form . Sed i mentary rock is made up of lots of other rocks, or even animal remains( Fossils), all stuck together. Sedimentary rocks are built up of particles laid down as layers or beds of sediment and are later buried , compressed, a nd cemented into a solid mass . Examples: Sandstone, shale, limestone. Sedimentary rocks often have a layered appearance. Metamorphic Rocks Metamorphic rocks are igneous or sedimentary rocks that have been changed by heat, pressure, or both. Metamorphic rocks are usually formed deep within the Earth, during a process such as mountain building. Examples: Schist, slate, marble. The R ock Cycle O ver many years rock change from one type to another. This is called the rock cycle. Rocks can be changed by the weathering, erosion, heating, cooling and pressure. Weathering is the breaking down or dissolving of rocks and minerals on Earth ’ s surface. Water, ice, acids, salt, plants, animals, and changes in temperature are all cause s of weathering. Once the rock has been broken down, a process called erosion transports the bits of rock and minerals away. No rock on Earth’s surface is hard enough to resist weathering. Together, the processes of weathering and erosion carved the Grand Canyon, in the U.S. state of Arizona. What is the difference between rocks and minerals? 2 . People mined minerals from the ground to use as they were found, particularly gemstones, and later mined ores to extract metals such as Gold, Copper or Iron. In fact ages of human civilisation have been named after the mineral ores used — the Bronze Age and the Iron Age for example. A mineral is a naturally occurring solid that has a regular crystal structure and chemical make-up. Some minerals are made up of only one kind of atom. These minerals are called ‘native’ minerals and include gold and silver. Other minerals are made up of several or many different types of atoms. The mineral quartz (SiO,) is made up of molecules consisting of one atom of silicon (Si) and two atoms of oxygen (O). Quartz forms regular 18-sided crystals. Quartz is the most common mineral in the Earth’s crust. Gypsum Calcite Quartz There are over 3000 different minerals and many of these are common in rocks, however there are only about eight very common rock-forming minerals. Examples of common rock forming minerals include quartz, feldspar, mica, olivine and calcite. Some rocks are made up of several minerals (e.g. Granite) and some rocks are made of only one mineral (e.g. limestone). The appearance of rocks depends mainly on the type of minerals that make it up and the way the rock has been formed. Some rocks are made up of other broken down rocks that have been ‘cemented’ together and some are formed from interlocking crystals. The size of the mineral crystals or grains in rocks varies from very large (crystals about 5mm in granite) to microscopic (as in shale) making them very hard to see and identify. Mineral crystals are easiest to identify in rocks formed from slowly cooling molten rock deep under ground. Why are dark-colo red peppered moths rare today? ______________________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________________ Directions: Answer the following question in a paragraph on a separate sheet of paper. Use the following words in your paragraph: variation , adaptation , and natural selection . 6. How is the peppered moth story an example of natural selection? Answer KEY Peppered Moth Worksheet 1. What does variation mean? Variation means that individual organisms have different traits from one another. 2. What variation in peppered moths does the article describe? The article describes different colors: a dark-colored and a light-colored peppered moth. 3. Why were dark-colored peppered moths successful during the Industrial Revolution in England? Dark-colored peppered moths were successful during the Industrial Revolution in England because air pollution killed the gray lichens that covered trees and the dark bark showed through. The dark-colored moths were harder for predators to spot. 4. What do you think would have happened to the peppered moth population during the Industrial Revolution if a dark variet y of the species had not existed ? Answers may vary. Sample answer: I think that the peppered moths in England might have all died if the dark variety did not exist. 5. Why are dark-colo red peppered moths rare today? Dark-colored peppered moths are rare today because the environment is cleaner and the lichens have returned to the trees. Light-colored peppered moths survive better on the light trees. Directions: Answer the following question in a paragraph on a separate sheet of paper. Use the following words in your paragraph: variation , adaptation , and natural selection . 6. How is the peppered moth story an example of natural selection? Peppered moths have variation in their color. Some are light grey and some are dark. The dark color is an adaptation that allowed the moths to blend in and hide on trees with dark bark. The moths with the dark color were more likely to survive and reproduce because they were not eaten by other animals as often as those with light color. For that reason, dark colored moths became more common over time.

uploads/science/SBD balancing equations.searchText: Activity sheet 1 . 4 Rules for balancing equations and writing formulae for ionic compounds Rules for balancing equations 1. Write a word equation for the reaction. 2. Write the formula for each substance using the rules for covalent or ionic substances. 3. Balance the equation by putting numbers in front of formulae so that the numbers of atoms of each element is the same on reactant and product sides. Do this in the following order: (i) Balance metal atoms (ii) Balance non-metal atoms (iii) Balance hydrogen atoms (iv) Balance oxygen atoms (v) Add subscripts for states (s), (l), (g) or (aq). 1. Balance the following equations by adding numbers in front of formulae: a. Mg (s) + H 2 O (i) Mg(OH) 2(aq) + H 2(g) b. H 2 S (g) + H 2 SO 4(aq) S (s) + SO 2(g) + H 2 O (l) c. FeCl 2(aq) + Cl 2(g) FeCl 3(aq) d. Fe (s) + HNO 3(aq) Fe(NO 3 ) 2( aq) + H 2(g) e. ( NH 4 ) 2 SO 4(aq) + BaCl 2(aq) NH 4 Cl (aq) + BaSO 4(s) f. CH 4(g) + O 2(g) CO 2(g) + H 2 O (l) g. Al (s) + Cl 2(g) AlCl 3(s) h. Zn (s) + HNO 3(aq) Zn(NO 3 ) 2(aq) + H 2(g) 2. Write balanced equations for the following reactions. a. calcium + oxygen solid calcium oxide b. hydrogen chloride gas + sodium hydroxide solution sodium chloride solution + water c. sodium + water sodium hydroxide + hydrogen d. magnesium carbonate powder magnesium oxide powder + carbon dioxide e. sodium + oxygen solid sodium oxide f. zinc + copper(II)sulfate solution zinc(II)sulfate solution + copper g. zinc + hydrochloric acid zinc(II)chloride solution + hydrogen 3. Write equations to represent the following reactions. a. Dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution react to produce a solution of sodium chloride and water. b. Burning carbon in a limited amount of oxygen produces carbon monoxide gas. c. Dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium carbonate solution react to produce a solution of sodium chloride, carbon dioxide and water. d. Sodium hydroxide solution is added to dilute sulfuric acid to produce a solution of sodium sulfate and water. e. Solutions of potassium iodide and lead(II)nitrate are mixed to form a precipitate of lead iodide and potassium nitrate solution. f. Copper metal is added to hydrochloric acid to produce copper(II)chloride solution and hydrogen. g. Sulfur dioxide gas reacts with oxygen to produce sulfur trioxide gas. h. Solid calcium carbonate decomposes when heated to form solid calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas. Nitrogen monoxide reacts with oxygen to produce nitrogen dioxide gas. j. Calcium bromide and ammonium carbonate solutions react to produce a precipitate of calcium carbonate and ammonium bromide solution. k. Dinitrogen tetroxide gas decomposes to form nitrogen dioxide gas. Rules for writing formulae for ionic compounds. 1. Check that the compound is ionic (made from a metal and non-metal ion). 2. Write the symbols for each element 3. Find the valency for each ion by using the Periodic Table, table of polyatomic ions or Roman numerals in the name of the compound. 4. Use the cross-over method to determine how many of each type of ion is needed to make the total charge zero. 5. Write the formula using subscripts (numbers at the bottom of symbols). Note: For two ions of valency 2 e.g. Mg 2 + and O 2 -, only one ion of each type is needed and the formula is MgO. Do not write 1 as a subscript – the absence of a subscript means that there is only one of this ion. 6. If there are two or more polyatomic ions in the formula, then the whole ion is enclosed in brackets and the subscript is outside the brackets. e.g. magnesium nitrate is Mg(NO 3 ) 2 Now work through the questions. (M) hydrochloric acid HCl sulfuric acid H2SO4 nitric acid HNO3 16. Write the name and formula of the weak organic acid present in vinegar. Ethanoic acid CH3COOH 17. What is the definition of a base? A base is a substance that neutralises an acid 18. What is the definition of an alkali? A soluble base 19. (a) When you put a zinc into acid an invisible gas called hydrogen is made. What is the name and formula of a common strong alkali used in the lab. Sodium hydroxide NaOH 21. We often refer to sodium hydroxide as caustic soda. What is the meaning of caustic? Capable of burning, dissolving or corroding by chemical action. 22. A common weak alkali used in the lab is actually a solution made by dissolving a smelly gas in water. What is it called? Ammonia 23. Two solutions have lost their labels but one of them is vinegar and the other is caustic soda. Explain how you would discover which was which? Add an acid-base indicator to each solution. Vinegar will be the acid and caustic soda will be the base. 24. Some text books suggest that litmus indicator has a purple colour in water. How would you account for this? The purple colour is a mixture of the red and blue colours which are present in equal amounts in neutral water. 25. A solution of hydrochloric acid has a pH of 1. As the acid is diluted its pH will rise Use this idea to suggest how acid spills should be treated. When acids are reacted with carbonates and bicarbonates a colourless gas is given off. (a) What is the name of this gas? Carbon dioxide (b) Describe how you would test for this gas. Turns limewater milky

Explain why a falling object will reach a constant speed of fall (Terminal velocity). As the object falls, the drag force (air resistance)e acting on it increases with speed. At the terminal velocity, the drag force is equal and opposite to the weight force and the object stops accelerating. 4. The forwards in a Provincial rugby team have the following masses: 120kg, 110kg, 105kg 100kg, 98kg, 95kg, 90kg and 90kg. Calculate the total mass of the pack and also what this forward pack would weigh in Newtons. Total mass = 808kg. The weight force on this = 808 x 10 = 8080 N 5. Write a definition for weight. Weight is the force of gravity on a mass. 6. Draw and label all the forces acting on the rock. 7. Draw and label all the forces acting on the skyrocket. 8. In the following diagrams calculate the net force on the 1 kg trolleys and also their acceleration. (a) Nett Force = 3 N to the right Acceleration = 3 ms-2 (b) Nett Force = 9 N to the left Acceleration = 9 ms-2 (c) Nett Force = 10 N to the right Acceleration = 10 ms-2 9. “An object will not accelerate when the forces acting on it are balanced”. uploads/science/Sc 1.6 #6 Answers.doc.searchText: ﻿SCIENCE 1.6 Name: ANSWERS WORKSHEET SIX TYPES AND TRANSFER OF ENERGY Ep = mgh Ek = ½mv2 1. What is the unit for energy? Joules What is the symbol for this unit? J 2. List the names of six types of energy. Heat, Kinetic, Gravitational potential, Solar, Sound, Elastic potential, Chemical potential. 3. Name the main type(s) of energy present in the following situations. (a) An unlit match. Chemical potential energy (b) A stretched rubber band Elastic potential energy (c) An orbiting satellite Kinetic energy, Gravitational potential energy (d) A thunder clap Sound energy (e) A bolt of lightning Electrical energy and light energy (f) A kicked soccer ball Kinetic energy 4. The sun is a giant hydrogen bomb. It uses nuclear energy to create solar energy. This solar energy is a mixture of different types of radiant energy such as light and heat . This radiant energy can travel through space to earth and the earth absorbs some of it and reflects some of it. Plants use chlorophyll to absorb light energy except for the colour green which they reflect. They store this energy in their leaves and roots as chemical potential energy. 5. Write energy transfer equations for the following situations. (a) An electric bell is switched on. Electrical energy Kinetic energy Sound energy (b) A bullet is fired up into the air. Chemical potential energy Kinetic energy Gravitational PE (c) A pine-cone falls off the top of a pine tree. Gravitational potential energy Kinetic energy 6. Usually when energy is transferred from one type to another , some of the energy is also turned into Heat . In a car motor, less than 50% of the chemical energy stored in the petrol is turned into the kinetic energy of the moving car. The car engine gets very hot and this unusable heat must be removed. The car radiator is filled with water which circulates through the motor and removes the heat. The hot water then circulates through the radiator and is cooled by the air passing over it. 7. In each of the following pairs, one member of the pair has more energy. Which is it? (a) A kg of lead and a kg of feathers on the same shelf. Same (b) A 50cent piece on a table or a 50cent piece on the ground beside it? Table (c) A cricket-ball hit by Noddy or a cricketball hit by Superman?? Superman 8. Calculate the gravitational potential energy in a 1.6 kg pot-plant which is on a shelf 1.4 m above the floor. (Use g = 10 Nkg-1) E = mgh = 1.6 x 10 x 1.4 = 22.4 J 9. Calculate the gravitational potential energy in a 0.4kg seagull which is flying at a height of 200 m above the ground. (Use g = 10 Nkg-1) E = mgh = 0.4 x 10 x 200 = 800 J 10. Calculate what height a 3kg object must have above the ground if it has 540J of gravitational potential energy? (Use g = 10 Nkg-1) E = mgh 540 = 3 x 10 x h h = 18 m 11. A boy and his bike have a combined mass of 70 kg. If the boy is cycling at 15ms-1 how much kinetic energy is present? E = ½mv2 = ½ x 70 x 152 = 7875 J 12. A bullet with mass 15g is fired at 200ms-1. How much kinetic energy has it got? E = ½mv2 = ½ x 0.015 x 2002 = 300 J 13. A 200g orange falls off a tree and just before it hits the ground it reaches a speed of 10 ms-1. (a) Calculate how much kinetic energy it has. E = ½mv2 = ½ x 0.2 x 102 = 10 J (b) Calculate how high it was growing on the tree before it fell off. (HARD!) E = mgh 10 = 0.2 x 10 x h h = 5 m

uploads/science/Sea Floor Spreading Acti.searchText: Name: Date: Period: Modeling sea floor spreading Summary In this activity students will use actual data from historic oceanographic cruises to examine sea floor spreading. They will also model sea floor spreading at a spreading center such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Learning Objectives At the completion of this activity you should be able to : • Plot data on a diagram. • Draw conclusions from the data. • Make predictions about future events related to this data. Materials • Student Handout • Posterboard / cardstock • Paper • Scissors Background Using actual data from the Glomar Challenger cruises will allow you to see a real-world connection between classroom science and “real” science. Also, creating a model for sea flo or spreading will allow you to see a hands-on example of this phenomenon. Procedure Part 1 To create a working model of sea floor spreading, follow the model seen below (Figure 1) . The base is best if made from poster board or card stock. The width and length of the base are not critical, as long as they are at least 12 cm wide and 30 cm long. Cut 3 slits, each slightly more than 8 cm wide. One slit needs to be in the center, and the other two at either end of the base, at least 4 cm in from the ends. Label the slits A and B at either end. Cut out the plate strips and place them back to back (marked sides together with number 1 at the top) and tape the end as indicated (at the end nearest number 7. ) Shade alternating strips to represent the reversals of the earth’s magnetic field. Be sure that the shading on either side of the strip match the alternate side. Put the two strips up through the bottom slit and then off to the slits at either end of the base. (Figure 2.) Thread the two strips through the center slit of the base, keeping the taped edge at the bottom. Pull the “North American Plate” strip down through slit “A” and the “Eurasian Plate” strip through slit “B”. Push the strips up from below until you can see numbers 3, 4, and 5 on top of the base. Templates for plate strips Analysis and Conclusion: 2209800 23495 0 0 Use the data below and write the age of the sediments found at each site on the map below. (Write the age on the line by each site.) Then answer the questions on the next page. -180975 167005 0 0 (Please write in complete sentences!) 1. Where are the youngest sediments found, compared to the Mid-Atlantic Ridge? 2. Where are the oldest sediments found? 3. Does the data support the theory of sea floor spreading? How? Use your spreading model to help you answer the following questions: 4. What are you modeling by pushing the strips up through the base? 5. What is being modeled at slits A and B as you pull the strips down through the base? 6. This model shows what happens at sea floor spreading centers, such as the mi d-Atlantic Ridge. List at least 2 good points of this model. 7. What are at least 2 reasons why this model is not a good model? 8. Seafloor spreading is continuing today along mid-ocean ridges such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Predict what effect this will have on the size of the ocean basin: Calculate the rate of movement in cm per year for the six pairs of peaks. Use the 2981325 10795 0 0 Formula rate = distance/time. Convert kilometers to centimeters. Example; Using the data, calculate the speed of the movement of the plates, in centimeters per year. ( Show your work! ) The North American Plate and the Eurasian Plate are moving apart at approximately_____________ cm per year. Enrichment: Studying Seafloor Spreading on Land Hopefully you are beginning to see how seafloor spreading changes the ocean floor. You should know that magma rises at the mid-ocean ridge and flows away from the ridge forming new oceanic crust . In g eneral, this activity is hidden beneath the ocean’s water. But there is a place where seafloor spreading can be seen on land. 1. What is the name of the landmass through which the mid-ocean ridge in the Atlantic Ocean passes? Where is it located? 2. How do the land structures of Iceland help confirm seafloor spreading? 3. Why do you think geologists might find Iceland a useful place to conduct research on seafloor spreading?

uploads/science/Sedimentary rocks Compre.searchText: ﻿ The formation of sedimentary rocks varies so there are a variety of sedimentary rocks. All of these rocks require a very long time for the processes of weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction and cementation to occur. These processes can take millions of years. Three types of sedimentary rocks are formed when weathered rock particles, organisms die or precipitated particles are compacted and cemented together. These three types of rocks are referred to as clastic sedimentary rock, organic sedimentary rock and chemical sedimentary rock, respectively. Clastic sedimentary rocks consist of smaller rocks cemented together. Examples include conglomerate and brecchia. Organic sedimentary rock is formed when organisms die and layers form that are eventually covered by clastic sedimentary rock and compressed. Examples include coal and limestone. Chemical sedimentary rocks form as a result of a chemical reaction that produces a precipitation. Banded iron formations (BIF) are chemical sedimentary rocks that contain iron oxide layers and are usually composed of the minerals magnetite and hematite. uploads/science/Sickle cell anaemia info.searchText: ﻿Sickle cell anaemia Cells in tissues need a steady supply of oxygen to work well. Normally, haemoglobin in red blood cells takes up oxygen in the lungs and carries it to all the tissues of the body. Red blood cells that contain normal haemoglobin have a biconcave shape (like a doughnut without a hole). This shape allows the cells to be flexible so that they can move through large and small blood vessels to deliver oxygen. Sickle haemoglobin is not like normal haemoglobin. It can form stiff rods within the red cell, changing it into a crescent, or sickle shape. Sickle-shaped cells are not flexible and can stick to vessel walls, causing a blockage that slows or stops the flow of blood. When this happens, oxygen can’t reach nearby tissues. Normal Red Cells and Sickle Red Cells Figure A shows normal red blood cells flowing freely in a blood vessel. The inset image shows a cross-section of a normal red blood cell with normal haemoglobin. Figure B shows abnormal, sickled red blood cells blocking blood flow in a blood vessel. The inset image shows a cross-section of a sickle cell with abnormal (sickle) haemoglobin forming abnormal stiff rods.

uploads/science/Simple Machines.docx.searchText: Simple Machines A simple machine is a simple tool that makes work easier. Compound machines have multiple simple machines working together to make work easier. In science, work is defined as force acting on an object to move it across a distance. Pushing, pulling and lifting are all common forms of work. There are 6 simple machines. Inclined Plane An inclined plane is a surface that is set at an angle to the horizontal. It allows objects to be raised with les effort than would be needed to lift it straight up. Ramps are used in shopping centres and other buildings to allow wheelchairs and prams to be raised with less effort. Although smaller effort needs to be made, a greater distance must be travelled. Ramps, hills and slides are examples of inclined planes. Wedge A wedge is made from two inclined planes with their horizontal edges together. The sloped sides of the inclined planes meet to form a sharp edge. This edge can be used to split things apart by reducing the force needed to cut through the object . Knives, axes and nails are examples of wedges. Screw Take an inclined plane and wrap it around a cylinder. Its sharp edge becomes another simple tool: the screw. It is a curved ramp. However, instead of an object being pushed up the ramp, the ramp is pushed down into the object. Car jacks use a large screw to lift huge loads with little effort. Jar lids, jacks, clamps and spiral staircases are examples of screws. Lever Any tool that prises something loose is a lever. A lever is a board or bar that rests on a turning point. This turning point is called the fulcrum. An object the lever moves is called the load. The closer the load is to the fulcrum, the easier it is to move. First-class L evers In a first class lever, the fulcrum lies between the effort and the load. First-class levers are force multipliers. They allow you to move a large load with a small force. Some first-class levers are crowbars and seesaws. Second-class L evers Second-class levers are also force multipliers; however, the load is between the fulcrum and the effort. Some second-class levers are wheelbarrows and nutcrackers. Third-class Levers Levers with the effort between the fulcrum and the load are called third-class levers. This type of lever is not a force multiplier, they are a speed multiplier. Some third-class levers are cricket bats, brooms and tennis racquets. Wheel and Axle The wheel and axle can move objects across distances. The whe el , the turns the axle, a cylindrical post attached to the centre of the wheel, which causes movement. A wheel and axle is a force multiplier. You apply a small effort to the wheel to move a large load with the axle. They can also be used to make things move faster. A ceiling fan is a wheel and axle. A large force is applied to the axle. Each time the axle turns the fan blades move a much greater distance in the same amount of time. Door knobs, gears and clocks and fans are examples of wheel and axles. Pulley s Instead of an axle, the wheel could also rotate a rope or cord. In a pulley, a cord wraps around a wheel. As the wheel rotates, the cord moves. If a hook is attached to the cord, the wheel’s rotation can be used to raise or lower objects. A single, fixed pulley can be used to make lifting a load easier. It does not decrease the amount of force needed to lift the load, but changes the direction of the effort. Using more than one pulley will decrease the force needed to lift the load. Flag poles, blinds and cranes are examples of pulleys. Practical Activities Inclined Planes Aim: To examine the relationship between forces and distance on inclined planes. Equipment: Small stack of textbooks or a dictionary Wooden board Set of slotted masses 5N spring balance Procedure: Place the textbooks in a pile. Place the slotted masses next to the pile of books and use the spring balance to slowly lift the mass so that its base is level with the top of the pile. Record the force measured by the spring balance. Lean the ramp against the pile of books to make a long, gentle slope. Place the slotted masses at the bottom of the ramp and use the spring balance to slowly pull it until its far end reaches the top of the pile. Record the force measured on the spring balance. Turn the wooden board around so it makes a short, steep ramp. Place the slotted masses at the bottom of the ramp and use the spring balance to slowly pull it until its far end reaches the top of the pile. Record the force measured on the spring balance. Change the height of the stack of books and repeat the process with two different heights. Height of books (cm) Length of gentle slope (cm) Length of steep slope (cm) Force used to lift straight up (N) Force used for gentle slope (N) Force used for steep slope (N) Results: Questions: Does it take more force to lift the mass straight up or along the ramp? In which case does the mass have to move further? Which method of raising the mass is better? Why? Look at your measurements of force and distance. Can you see a pattern? Wedges Aim: To observe the action of different wedges in separating wooden blocks. Equipment: 2 blocks of wood 2 elastic bands 2 wooden wedges, one blunt and one sharp Procedure: Use the elastic bands to hold the two blocks of wood together. Try to pull the two blocks of wood apart with your fingers. Now, use the blunt wedge to separate the two blocks. Now, try using the sharp wedge to separate the blocks. Questions: Could you separate the blocks of wood easily with just your fingers? Using the blunt wedge, was it easier or harder to separate the blocks than with just your fingers? Is it easier or harder to separate the two blocks with the sharp wedge than with just your fingers? Which edge made separating the two blocks easiest? Screws Aim: To observe the action of a moving inclined plane, the screw. Equipment: Self-tapping screw Block of wood Screwdriver Procedure: Try to push the screw into the wooden block with your hand. Now use the screwdriver to fix the screw halfway into the wood by turning it Questions: Were you able to get the screw into the wooden block by just pushing it? How does the thread (the inclined plane) on the screw allow you to get the screw in the block? Wheels and Axles Aim: To observe the advantages provided by the wheel and axle. Equipment: Screw embedded in a block of wood Screw driver Procedure: Try to remove the screw from the block of wood by turning the shaft instead of the handle. Remove the screw by using the screwdriver as it is meant to be used, by turning the handle. Questions: Can the screw be removed by turning the shaft of the screwdriver instead of the handle? What difference does using the handle of the screwdriver make to the effort needed to turn the screw? During one full turn of the screwdriver, which moves further – the outside edge of the handle or the outside edge of the shaft? Is a screwdriver a force multiplier or a speed multiplier? Explain your choice. ‘A fan is a speed multiplier.’ Explain what this statement means. Levers Aim: To examine the relationship between forces and distances in first-class levers. Equipment: 30 cm wooden ruler Pencil Blu -tack 8 x 50g masses Procedure: Use the blu -tack to hold the pencil to the bench. Lay the ruler across the pencil so that it balances in the middle (15 cm) . Place three masses 12cm from the fulcrum (on the 3cm mark) . This is the load. Look at the picture below if you are not sure. One at a time place masses on the other end of the ruler until the load is lifted. This is the effort. Record the number masses needed to lift the load. Move the load 4cm closer to the fulcrum and repeat step 4. Move the load another 4 cm closer to the fulcrum and repeat step 4. Load (12 cm from fulcrum) Record your results in the table. Repeat the process for four masses. Effort Fulcrum Results: Load (number of masses) Distance from Fulcrum (cm) Effort (number of masses) 3 12 cm 3 8 cm 3 4 cm 4 12 cm 4 8 cm 4 4 cm Questions: Describe any pattern you can see in the data you have collected. Why is this type of lever called a force multiplier? Would there be any advantage to using this type of lever to raise a light load with a large effort? Explain your answer. Pulleys Aim: To examine the relationships between forces and distances in pulley systems. Equipment: 2 triple pulleys 1 metre length of string Set of slotted masses 5 N spring balance Retort stand Boss head and clamp 2 bricks Procedure: Set up the retort stand, boss head and clamp so that the boss had and clamp is at the very top. Extend the clamp so that it is at the very end. Place the retort stand on the edge of the bench and put the bricks on the base to weigh it down. Attach one pulley to the slotted masses and use the spring balance to find its weight, in newtons. This weight is the load that is to be lifted. Attach the piece of string to the top of the pulley attached to the masses. Thread the string through the lowest pulley at the top. Look at diagram one to help you. Attach the spring balance to the end of the string and pull on the balance slowly so that the load is lifted 10 cm upwards. Record the force on the spring balance. This is the effort. Also record how far you had to pull the string to lift the load. Now arrange the system with 2, 3 and 4 pulleys and record the effort needed to lift the load 10 cm. Use the diagrams to help you thread the systems. uploads/science/simple_machines_year_10_.searchText: Simple Machines Levers Simple machines can change the direction or size of a force by using ‘mechanical advantage’ to multiply force. A lever is balanced on a fulcrum, which allows it to pivot. A load is lifted by placing effort on another part of the lever. A lever involves moving a load around a pivot using effort (or a force). Examples of tools that are classified as levers include scissors, pliers, hammer claws and tongs. Levers are a simple machine that increase force For a tool to be classed as a lever there must be:  a rigid handle  a fulcrum (or pivot) around which the handle rotates  a force increase – caused by the distance from the effort force to the fulcrum being larger than the load force to the fulcrum 124 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Levers are a simple machine that increase force Levers are classified in classes depending on the position of the effort and load in relation to the fulcrum.  Seesaw type Lever (Class 1): A lever where the load force acts on the opposite side of the fulcrum to the effort force. Examples include a Crowbar, Hammer and Tyre iron  Wheelbarrow type lever (class 2): A lever where the load force acts on the same side of the fulcrum as the effort force. Examples include a Wheelbarrow, a Spanner and a Ratchet /tiedown  Inclined Planes An inclined plane is a simple machine and it can be used to reduce the effort required to move a load. If the slope has a small angle, then a person has to push or pull the object over a longer distance to reach a height, but with very little effort. If the slope is steep, with a greater angle, a person must push or pull the object over a very short distance to reach the same height, but with more effort. Mechanical advantage is calculated by length of slope divided by height of the slope. There is a greater mechanical advantage if the slope is gentle because then less force will be needed to move an object up (or down) the slope. 125 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Simple machines Review 1. Label the diagram below with fulcrum, effort force and load force 2. Using the information above – how much force (N) does the boy need to use to lift the box? EXTENSION Load force (L) x d = Effort force (E) x D 3. uploads/science/Slime mould investigatio.searchText: ﻿Mercy College Year Eight Science Slime Mould Investigation What are Slime Moulds? Slime moulds are a group of small encrusting moulds consisting of over 500 species. Slime moulds are normally found in cool shady moist places on rotting logs, leaf litter or moist organic soils. They can grow to a few 100 millimetres in size and are often brightly coloured. They feed on bacteria, decaying/rotting organic matter and other microscopic organic material. The group has in the past been regarded as “of uncertain origin” and also classified as both a fungus and an animal. It is now considered as a member of the Kingdom Protista. Its life cycle starts as a spore cell (like a fungus), which can be distributed widely by air and water, and this develops into a .single celled multinucleate plasmodium (or large bag of cytoplasm). This stage can travel by a process of protoplasmic streaming towards food sources, which it then engulfs and consumes. The rate of movement/growth can be as much as 30mm/hour. The plasmodium grows best in moist areas with temperatures below 25C. If environmental conditions deteriorate (too cold, hot, or dry) they will move into an irreversible spore-forming reproductive stage. This investigation will use the slime mould Physarum polycephalum, as it easy to grow on agar plates. It is harmless to humans; but the specimen and agar should not be touched as this will introduce other microbes to the agar medium and possibly ruin the experiment. Oat flakes (think porridge) have been used as the basic food source to grow the specimens. Remarkably the slime can “sense” where the food is and move towards it (like an animal). Instructions for the Investigation The aim of the investigation is to determine what factors affect the growth of the mould. Food types, food quantity, distance of food from the initial specimen, and light intensity may all affect the speed and strength of growth. Note: The agar provides constant moisture conditions and varying the temperature is likely to result in the specimen stopping any further growth. In bench groups (of 3-4 students) plan what is to be tested (rate of growth, type of food etc) and complete the Planning Section. Each student will then get a sample of slime mould growing on an agar plate in a Petri dish. Depending on what they are testing they can also get different types of food. Measurements should then be taken over a couple of days to record the growth rate and observe the directions etc. Specimens can be taken home to record the growth over a period of several hours. Measurements should be taken to the nearest ½ mm with a clear ruler. Data should be collected in tabular form and can then be processed and displayed on graphs or using Excel spreadsheet charts. Evaluations can then be completed onto a final copy sheet for assessment. The Planning process is a group activity, but the Conducting of the experiment (all measurements) and Processing (plotting) should be individual work. In evaluating the investigation you can refer to the results of other group members to compare and contrast growth. A final copy of the investigation can then be written-up for handing in and assessment. uploads/science/Specific heat capacity c.searchText: ﻿Specific Heat Capacity Activity 1: Heating Substances in the Sun The following table shows the temperature after 10g of four different substances have been in direct sunlight for 60 minutes. Time (mins) Air (⁰C) Water (⁰C) Sand (⁰C) Metal (⁰C) 0 25 25 25 25 15 29 26 30 35 30 33 28 35 45 45 36 29 40 55 60 40 30 45 65 Create a line graph for each substance on the grid below. Put the time on the x-axis (along the bottom) and the temperature on the y-axis (up the side). Don’t forget to give your graph a title. 1. Order the substances based on the time required to heat them from slowest to fastest. 2. Which do you think will cool the fastest? Explain your choice. 3. When you boil water in a pot on the stove, which heats up faster, the metal or the water? Explain your choice. 4. The specific heat capacity is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of 1g of a substance by 1⁰C. A substance with a high specific heat capacity heats up more slowly than one with a low specific heat capacity because it needs to absorb more energy before it heats up. a. Which of the four substances has the highest heat capacity? Explain your choice. b. Which of the four substances has the lowest heat capacity? Explain your choice. 5. The specific heat capacities of the four substances are 4200J/kg/⁰C, 880J/kg/⁰C, 1000J/kg/⁰C and 400J/kg/⁰C. Match each specific heat capacity to one of the substances. a. Air = __________ b. Water = __________ c. Sand = __________ d. Metal = __________ 6. Assuming they both start at the same temperature, which will heat up faster in the sun, a bottle of water or a swimming pool full of water? Explain your choice. Activity 2: Calculate the amount of heat absorbed or released (show all working) 1. A pot is filled with 9kg of water at 10oC. Calculate how much heat energy would be needed to raise the temperature to 60oC. [ specific heat capacity of water = 4200J/kg/⁰C ] 2. A girl is hiking in the bush and has a 2litre bottle of water, which weighs 2kg, in her backpack. The water gets heated by the sun and its temperature increases by 5⁰C. How much energy has it absorbed? 3. If the temperature of 3.5kg of water increases from 50⁰C to 100⁰C, how much water has been absorbed by the water? 4. How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of a 2kg bar of gold from 25⁰C to 85⁰C? [ specific heat capacity of gold = 130J/kg/⁰C ] 5. Half a kilogram of water at room temperature (25⁰C) is put in the freezer until it freezes at 0⁰C. How much heat energy has it released? 6. An iron object weighing 4kg was accidentally left outside in the sun. When it was brought inside, its temperature was 45⁰C. How much energy will it lose once it has cooled to room temperature? [ specific heat capacity of iron = 440J/kg/⁰C ]
