uploads/science/Speed and Acceleration u.searchText: Speed and Acceleration using a Ticker Timer coil magnet ticker tape power input ( a.c .) vibrating bar carbon paper disc A ticker timer is a piece of equipment which can be used to measure speed and acceleration. The ticker timer has a bar which vibrates at a known frequency of 50 times per second. A piece of ticker tape is passed under the bar and a carbon paper disc is threaded between the bar and the ticker tape. There is a small nodule at the end of the bar which produces a dot each time it hits the tape. The time between each dot is 1/50 th of a second, or 0.02 seconds. By measuring the distance between 6 dots (5 spaces) and dividing by the time taken (0.02 x 5 = 0.1 sec) the average speed can be calculated. Look at the ticker tape below. Use the following method to calculate the speed the tape was moving. Draw a line through a dot near the left. Draw a second line through the fifth dot after that. Measure the distance between the dots in cm. Calculate the speed in cm per second by dividing by 0.1 seconds (the time it takes to make 5 dots) Try the two examples below To calculate acceleration using a ticker timer, you must calculate the average speed of multiple intervals on your ticker tape. Look at the ticker tape below. Speed = Change in speed = Calculate the acceleration of this ticker tape by Putting a line through the first dot. Put a line through every fifth dot after that. Use the method on the previous page to find the average speed between the first two lines. Repeat the process for the other 3 intervals to get the average speed for each interval. Find the change in speed between each interval. The acceleration is the change in speed divided by the time between the intervals, in this case 0.1 seconds. Try to find the acceleration of the ticker tapes below using the method above.

uploads/science/Spice Worksheet answers..searchText: Planetary atmospheres Worksheet answers 1. Which environment has the coldest average surface temperature? Titan (-180 °C) 2. Which environment has the greatest atmospheric pressure? Venus (about 90 bar) 3. Which solar system body has an average surface temperature that is most similar to Earth’s? Mars 4. Describe differences between the Earth’s atmosphere now and four billion years ago. The Earth’s atmosphere today is composed of 77% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 2% of other gases. The atmospheric composition of Earth 4 billion years ago shows higher amounts of carbon dioxide (45%) and less nitrogen (10%). 5. Titan contains compounds that scientists believe are similar to the building blocks of early life on Earth. What differences exist between Earth and Titan that prevent us from assuming there is life on Titan? Life on Earth exists in conditions that include an average surface temperature of 15 °C and an atmosphere which includes oxygen. Titan’s average surface temperature is -180 °C, which is too cold for most life forms on Earth. Titan also appears to have no oxygen, which is required by many life forms on Earth. One of the reasons for Titan’s very cold temperature is that it is much further away from the Sun than the Earth (it is one of Saturn’s moons). This means much less sunlight reaches the surface of Titan. This might affect the survival of life forms such as plants. 6. If found, what type of life is most likely to exist on Mars? Life on Mars would have to be well adapted to cold temperatures and high amounts of carbon dioxide. Perhaps a primitive form of plant life might exist on Mars, as conditions seem to be similar to those of Earth 4 billion years ago. 7. What challenges would humans be faced with if they decided to colonise: (a) Mars Temperature: it is very cold (-65 °C) and humans would need specialised living conditions, maybe similar to those used in Antarctica. A lack of breathable atmosphere would require some means of producing oxygen, and extracting water from ground-based frozen sources might be a challenge. (b) Titan Titan is extremely cold (-180 °C). This would require specialised living conditions because we don’t find conditions this extreme on Earth. The atmosphere is not breathable by humans and might contain poisonous gases. Water might be difficult to find, but perhaps not impossible (it could be frozen). Sunlight would be poor, and it might be difficult to cultivate plants for food as there is no carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. (c) Mercury Mercury’s average temperature is 180 °C, hotter than anywhere on Earth. Shielding humans from this extreme temperature and the solar radiation this close to the Sun would be a challenge. There is almost no atmospheric pressure on Mercury, so finding breathable air or water for drinking would probably be impossible. The temperature on Mercury means that there is probably no water to be found on the surface. © 2009 The University of Western Australia | for conditions of use see spice.wa.edu.au/usage | ast0421 | version 1.0 Life in the Solar System 3: Planetary atmospheres 1 (worksheet answers) | page 1 secondary teachers’ enrichment program (science)

What do you think a star is made of? _________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Stars are gaseous objects in space that give off light and heat. They are made mainly of hydrogen and helium, with traces of heavier elements such as boron, carbon and nitrogen. For example, our sun contains about 80% hydrogen and 19% helium, while the remaining 1% is made up of the heavier elements. Compared with the size of the Earth, the sizes of stars are enormous. The sun is over one million times the size of the Earth, while one of the largest stars, Canopus, is 80 000 times the size of our sun. 2. In the core of the sun, hydrogen nuclei join together (fuse) and release energy. This type of reaction is called nuclear fusion. What is released when hydrogen nuclei fuse together? _____________________________________________ The reaction that occurs in stars involves the fusion of hydrogen nuclei to produce helium. uploads/science/Static Electricity Over.searchText: ﻿STATIC ELECTRICITY Atomic Structure The structure of the atom has a cloud of electrons orbiting around a nucleus in energy shells. It is the outer electrons that are involved in the production of static electricity. Static Electricity Friction between two surfaces can rub electrons off one object and onto another. The object that gains electrons becomes negative - the other becomes positive. This produces static electricity. Static Electricity: stationary charges on an object. e.g. A plastic comb rubbed on a cotton cloth becomes positively charged by losing electrons. Interaction of Charges Charge Law: Similar charges repel each other while opposite charges attract each other. Examples of Static Electricity Lightning • Caused by the friction between the air and the clouds. • Convection currents within the cloud also cause ice particles to produce static charge. • Charge on the ground below the ground becomes oppositely charged. • Lightning is discharged to the ground or tallest structure with a large charge density. Pollution Control • Chimneys have special electrostatic traps to attract smoke particles. • This reduces the amount reaching the atmosphere. Getting "Zapped" • Moving cars build up a charge as they move through the air. • Passengers sometimes get "zapped" as they get out of the car and touch the metal part of the door. • The charged flows around the person to the Earth.

It is designed to be delivered by two scientists or science communicators visiting a school, but a teacher could use the materials themselves too. The lesson is intended to be flexible and is made up of a set of short modules, mixing group activities with presentation and facilitator-led discussion. This guide outlines how we have found the lesson to work best, but we hope you will adapt the details to suit your own needs. Please share your suggestions and experiences by posting your comments at www.eurostemcell.org/resources. You can also email us at www.eurostemcell.org/contact. The lesson does not assume any prior knowledge of stem cells, or any detailed knowledge of cell structure or function. uploads/science/Strawberry DNA extration.searchText: ﻿Biology –Strawberry DNA Extraction Lab Name:____________________ Date:___________Hr:_______ “You will never be able to eat a strawberry again without thinking of how much DNA is in it!” Background Information: Ripe strawberries are an excellent source for extracting DNA because they are easy to pulverize and contain enzymes called pectinase and cellulase that help to break down cell walls. And most important, strawberries have eight copies of each chromosome (they are octoploid), so there is a lot of DNA to isolate. The purpose of each ingredient in the procedure is as follows: • Dishwasher soap helps to dissolve the cell membrane, which is a lipid bilayer. • Sodium chloride helps to remove proteins that are bound to the DNA. It also helps to keep the proteins dissolved in the aqueous layer so they don’t precipitate in the alcohol along with the DNA. • Ethanol or isopropyl alcohol causes the DNA to precipitate. When DNA comes out of solution it tends to clump together, which makes it visible. Materials per student group: • 1 strawberry • 10 ml DNA Extraction Buffer (soapy salty water) • 10 ml ice cold 91% or 100% isopropyl alcohol • 1 Ziploc TM bag • 1 clear test tube • 1 funnel lined with a moistened paper towel Procedure: 1. Obtain 1 strawberry from the front lab bench. 2. Place strawberry into a Ziploc TM bag and seal shut. 3. Squish for 1 minute to completely squash the fruit. 4. Add 10 ml DNA Extraction Buffer (soapy salty water) and squish for another minute. Try not to make a lot of soap bubbles. 5. Filter the contents of your baggie through a moistened paper towel set in a funnel, and collect the liquid in a test tube. This will take a few minutes. Do not squeeze the paper towel. Collect about 3 ml liquid. 6. Add 10 ml of ice cold isopropyl alcohol to the strawberry liquid in the tube. Pour the isopropyl alcohol carefully down the side of the tube so that it forms a separate layer on top of the strawberry liquid. 7. Watch for about a minute. What do you see? You should see a white fluffy cloud at the interface between the two liquids. That’s DNA! 8. Rinse your funnel. Put the Ziploc TM bag and paper towel in the garbage. 9. Answer the analysis questions. BIOLOGY Name___________________ DNA Isolation Lab Hour______Date__________ Analysis Questions 1. A person cannot see a single cotton thread 100 feet away, but if you wound thousands of threads together into a rope, it would be visible at some distance. How is this statement an analogy to our DNA extraction? 2. The strawberry DNA precipitate looks like long and thin fibers, almost like spider webs. Would the DNA look the same if it had come from a human? Explain 3. If you wanted to look at your DNA, could you use the same method of extraction as you did for the strawberries? Why or why not? 4. Why can’t you see the double helix? 5. How does your DNA differ from one of your classmate’s? How is it similar? 6. How does your DNA differ from the strawberry’s DNA? How is it similar? 7. Would the DNA be the same in any cell in the human body? Explain

uploads/science/Structure of the Earth.d.searchText: ﻿GEOLOGY The Structure of the Earth a) Inside the Earth Scientists think that the Earth is composed of layers. The outermost layer is like a thin skin and it is called the crust. The crust is solid and it is composed of rocks and minerals. The crust is not an even layer; it is thickest where there are mountains ranges (and in general under the continents) and thinnest beneath the deep oceans. The average thickness of the crust is about 30 km; the distance to the centre of the Earth is about 6500 km. That is, the crust is very thin compared to the distance to the centre of the Earth. The temperature in the crust ranges from about 200C (at the surface) to about 5000C (at the bottom of the crust). That is, the deeper you go into the crust (and the Earth) the hotter is becomes. Beneath the crust is a much thicker layer called the mantle. The mantle is about 2900 km thick and the temperatures range from about 5000C to 20000C. These high temperatures are enough to melt rock, and so the mantle is made up of partially solid, partially liquid (molten) rock. Sometimes molten rock spills out onto the crust as lava. At the centre is the core which contains two main layers. The outer core is believe to be made of molten iron and nickel. It has a thickness of about 2270 km and a temperature of about 30000C. The inner core is thought to be made of solid iron and nickel. It has a radius of about 1300 km and a temperature of about 4000oC. b) Plate tectonics The theory of plate tectonics proposes that the outermost part of the earth, the crust, is divided into a number of rigid plates which move in relation to each other. There are six or seven major plates and a number of smaller ones. Both continents and ocean floors form the upper part of these plates. The Australian continent is on the Indian-Australian plate. The tectonic plates are thought to be floating on the upper potion of the mantle and their movement is thought to be due to convection currents (movement of the hot mantle material) caused by the tremendous heat within the earth. The boundaries of these plates were determined by mapping the positions of earthquake epicentres because earthquakes tend to occur where plates meet or move apart. Since the plates are moving with respect to each other, the edges or margins of the plates will be geologically unstable: i) where two plates are forced together i.e. they are colliding, one plate is often forced under the other. The plate that is forced underneath moves back into the mantle. Collision zones of plates, called subduction zones, are often associated with earthquakes, volcanoes, ocean trenches and fold mountains. This type of plate movement i.e. plate collision, is thought to have caused the formation of the Himalayas, in Asia, and the Andes mountains in South America. The ring of volcanoes around the Pacific ocean also is thought to be due to the Pacific plate is being pushed under other plates. ii) where plates are moving apart, new material from the mantle rises up to form new crust. Mid-ocean ridges (mountains), volcanoes and earthquakes are often associated with these areas. Two plates moving apart are thought to have caused the formation of the mid-Atlantic ridge, a mountain range under the Atlantic ocean. iii) where plates move past one another, faults, or breaks, occur in the rocks. This is called lateral movement of plates. Active volcanoes are absent in these areas, but severe earthquakes can occur as the two plates move in "jerky" movements past one another. This type of plate movement occurs along the western coast of North America, and it forms the San Andreas fault. As the plates move over the surface of the Earth, they carry the continents with them. It is thought that the continents were originally one land mass and over the billions of years they have slowly moved apart (and they are still moving!). c) Volcanoes Sometimes, due to pressure in the mantle layer, magma (molten rock) is forced through a weak part in the Earth's crust. When this happens, a volcano forms. The fluid magma which flows out of a volcano, over the surface, is called lava. "New" rock is formed when molten lava cools. Smoke, steam, ash and other gases also pour out of a volcano during an eruption. d) Mountain building The layers of rocks that make up the Earth’s crust are being continually pushed, twisted, split and folded by Earth movements. Mountains are often formed because of these tremendous forces exerted within and on the Earth’s crust: Folding of the crust can occur because of these forces. For example when two plates collide, fold mountains often form at the edge (or edges) of the plate. Most of the Earth’s mountain ranges have been formed this way. Another way in which rock layers may react to huge forces is by splitting or faulting. When a crack or a break forms in a layer of rocks, the rock on one side of the crack can move up, down or sideways, relative to the rock on the other side of the crack. This may result in one part of the Earth’s crust being higher compared to an adjacent part. Igneous Rocks Rocks which at one time were molten i.e. magma, are called igneous rocks. These rocks are composed of interlocking crystals. (Crystals are solids with a definite shape and straight, sharp edges) Igneous rocks can form from magma in two ways: i) when magma reaches the earth's surface, it becomes lava. Lava cools relatively quickly and produces igneous rock made up of small crystals. An example of rock formed this way is basalt. Basalt is normally a dark-coloured, hard rock. ii) at times, magma cools and solidifies below the Earth's surface . When this occurs, cooling is very slow, and the rock formed is composed of large crystals. An example of rock formed this way is granite. The magma which forms granite is too thick to be forced through weaknesses in the earth's crust, and it forms great domes underneath the surface. In time, the surrounding softer rocks are eroded, leaving the rounded domes of granite. Granite is a multicoloured rock composed of quite large interlocking crystals. Sedimentary Rocks a) Weathering Weathering is the process by which rocks are broken down into smaller pieces or changed to other substances when exposed to the atmosphere. This process is caused by contact of the exposed outermost parts of the rock with water, air and living things. Two types of weathering occur: i) Physical Weathering - this results in rock being broken down into smaller pieces (the composition of the rock is not changed). - physical weathering can be due to - temperature changes - action of frost or ice - abrasion by moving particles - action of plants and animals ii) Chemical Weathering - this results in the rocks being changed into different substances. - chemical weathering occurs when air and water come in contact with rock and a chemical reaction with the rock occurs - some of the chemicals in the environment that cause chemical weathering are: - carbonic acid, which is formed when carbon dioxide dissolves in water - humic acid, which is a weak acid formed from decaying plants in the soil. - oxygen and water b) Erosion Erosion is the process of removal of the weathered rock particles from the bedrock locality i.e. from the place where they were formed from the parent rock. The main agents of erosion are: i) water - moving water in the rivers, steams and in the ocean can transport rock particles from one place to another. The faster the movement of water, the larger the rock particles that can be moved. - water running over and through soil and rocks also causes erosion of small rock particles and soluble substances. ii) ice - a glacier is a very large river of ice and as it flows downhill it carves out a large valley by breaking off pieces of rock and carry them with it. iii) wind - the ability of wind to carry particles is less than that of water. However, wind can move much faster that water , and so can still carry quite large sand/rock particles. c) The formation of sedimentary rocks. The weathered materials carried by water, ice or wind in the process of erosion, will finally be "dropped" or deposited somewhere. This process is called deposition or sedimentation. The weathered material which is deposited during erosion is called sediment. Over time, different layers of sediment often form on top of one another. Layers of sediment can also be formed when a mixture of rocks and sand are deposited at the one time from the flowing water. The heaviest material will settle quickest i.e. it will form the bottom layer, then the next heaviest will settle etc. Thus layers, with the heaviest material at the bottom to the lightest as the top layer, will be formed. As sediment builds up, layer upon layer, it can be very slowly converted into rock, called a sedimentary rock. The process of forming many sedimentary rocks involves first compaction (pushing the particles in the sediment close together), and then secondly, the cementing of the particles together by chemicals. That is, in a sediment, the particles are just mixed together, but in a sedimentary rock, the particles are "cemented" together to form a solid piece of material. Some sedimentary rocks are formed from solids which have precipitated out of solution (salt), and other from remains of plants and animals that have been cemented together (limestone). Sometimes plants or animals e.g. shells, form part of a sediment. These dead plants and animals then become part of the sedimentary rock which forms. The remains or imprints of these plants and animals in the rock are referred to as fossils. d) Characteristics of sedimentary rocks i) Most sedimentary rocks have a layered structure. In a series of layered rock, normally the oldest (first deposited) rock is at the bottom, and the youngest (last to be deposited) is at the top. ii) Some sedimentary rocks show the remains of animals and plants trapped in the rock i.e. they contain fossils. iii) Many sedimentary rocks contain grains cemented together. iv) Sedimentary rocks are often much softer than igneous or metamorphic rocks. e) Some common sedimentary rocks Conglomerate - composed of large rounded pebbles (> 2mm in diameter) cemented together. Sandstone - composed of medium sized sand grains (< 2mm and visible to naked eye) Mudstone - composed of a mixture of silt and clay sized particles , cemented together Limestone - composed of calcium carbonate and is normally pale in colour - can be made of shell, coral or bone fragments cemented together - can be formed by the precipitation of calcium carbonate from aqueous solution Coal - black or brown solid composed mainly of carbon - formed from plant material that has been compressed under layers of sediment. Metamorphic Rocks When solid rock is subjected to heat and pressure in the earth's crust, it can change into a different rock. This new rock is called a metamorphic rock. Metamorphic rocks are often formed from rock which is formed or buried deep in the Earth's crust where there would be high temperatures and pressures. They are also formed in the crust in volcanic areas because the magma heats the surrounding rocks to sufficiently high temperatures to change them into metamorphic rocks. Metamorphic rocks are normally much harder than sedimentary rocks and they sometimes have visible grains. Examples of metamorphic rocks include: - marble - often white, has visible grains and is formed from limestone. - quartzite - very hard, has visible grains and is formed from sandstone. - gneiss - has visible grains and normally contains dark bands. It is formed from shale, which must first be changed into other metamorphic rocks before gneiss is finally formed. Marble and quartzite are normally formed in areas where the heat is supplied by volcanoes. However, gneiss is formed deep in the crust where high pressure and temperature conditions exist. uploads/science/studying pedigrees.doc.searchText: ﻿*Biology Name ___________________________ Date________________ Period_______ STUDYING PEDIGREES ACTIVITY Introduction: A pedigree is a visual chart that depicts a family history or the transmission of a specific trait. They can be interesting to view and can be important tools in determining patterns of inheritance of specific traits. Pedigrees are used primarily by genetic counselors when helping couples decide to have children when there is evidence of a genetically inherited disorder in one or both families. They are also used when trying to determine the predisposition of someone to carry a hereditary disease for example, familial breast cancer. The Components of a Pedigree: Squares are used to indicate males in a family. Circles are used to indicate females. If the individual is “affected" by the trait (dominant or recessive) we darken the shape. A line between a male and a female indicates a marriage or union. A line drawn down from the marriage line indicates offspring. Sometimes, you will see some shapes filled in only half way - this notation indicates a hybrid (heterozygous) or carrier of the trait. Read pages 396-397 (Sect. 14.1) in your textbook for more information. Analyzing Simple Pedigrees: A pedigree is just like a family tree except that it focuses on a specific genetic trait. A pedigree usually only shows the phenotype of each family member. With a little thought, and the hints below, you may be able to determine the genotype of each family member as well! Hints for analyzing pedigrees: 1) If the individual is homozygous recessive, then both parents MUST have at least one recessive allele (parents are heterozygous or homozygous recessive). 2) If an individual shows the dominant trait, then at least one of the parents MUST have the dominant phenotype. This one will be pretty obvious when you look at the pedigree. 3) If both parents are homozygous recessive, then ALL offspring will be homozygous recessive. NOTE: In a pedigree, the trait of interest can be dominant or recessive. The majority of harmful genetic conditions are only seen when an individual is homozygous recessive - examples of conditions caused by recessive alleles include cystic fibrosis (a disease of the secretory glands, including those that make mucus and sweat), Falconi anemia (a blood disorder), albinism (a lack of pigmentation), and phenylketonuria (a metabolic disorder). Some genetic conditions are caused by dominant alleles (and may therefore be expressed in homozygous dominant or heterozygous individuals)- examples of conditions caused by dominant alleles include polydactyly (presence of extra fingers), achondroplasia (a type of dwarfism), neurofibromatosis (a nervous disorder), and a disease known as familial hypercholesterolemia in which affected individuals suffer from heart disease due to abnormally high cholesterol levels Human Pedigrees For Questions 1-9, use the pedigree chart shown below. Some of the labels may be used more than once. ________ 1. A male 2. A female ________ 3. A marriage 4. A person who expresses the trait 5. A person who does not express the trait 6. A connection between parents and offspring ________ 7. How many generations are shown on this chart? Assuming the chart above is tracing the dominant trait of "White Forelock (F)" through the family. F is a tuft of white hair on the forehead. ________8. What is the most likely genotype of individual “A”? (FF, Ff or ff?) ________9. What is the most likely genotype of individual “C”? (FF, Ff or ff?) Example 1: Tracing the path of an autosomal recessive trait Trait: Falconi anemia Forms of the trait: • The dominant form is normal bone marrow function - in other words, no anemia. • The recessive form is Falconi anemia. Individuals affected show slow growth, heart defects, possible bone marrow failure and a high rate of leukemia. A typical pedigree for a family that carries Falconi anemia. Note that carriers are not indicated with half-colored shapes in this chart. Analysis Questions. To answer questions #1-5, use the letter "f" to indicate the recessive Falconi anemia allele, and the letter "F" for the normal allele. 1. What is Arlene's genotype? 2. What is George's genotype? 3. What are Ann & Michael's genotypes? 4. Most likely, Sandra's genotype is . 5. List three people from the chart (other than George) who are most likely carriers of Falconi anemia. *Example 2: Tracing the path of an autosomal dominant trait Trait: Neurofibromatosis Forms of the trait: • The dominant form is neurofibromatosis, caused by the production of an abnormal form of the protein neurofibromin. Affected individuals show spots of abnormal skin pigmentation and non-cancerous tumors that can interfere with the nervous system and cause blindness. Some tumors can convert to a cancerous form. • The recessive form is a normal protein - in other words, no neurofibromatosis. A typical pedigree for a family that carries neurofibromatosis is shown below. Note that carriers are not indicated with half-colored shapes in this chart. Use the letter "N" to indicate the dominant neurofibromatosis allele, and the letter "n" for the normal allele. Analysis Questions: 1. Is individual #1 most likely homozygous dominant or heterozygous? Explain how you can tell. 2. What is the genotype of individual #3? 3. Can you be sure of the genotypes of the affected siblings of individual #3? Explain. __________________ *YOUR TURN!! Instructions: 1. Draw a pedigree showing all the individuals described in the problem. (Include their names if given.) 2. Label the genotypes of as many individuals in the pedigree as possible. 3. Shade in half of the symbol if you know that the individual is heterozygous or a carrier. *Draw your own Pedigree - Case study #1: Condition of Interest: Albinism Albinism is a condition in which there is a mutation in one of several possible genes, each of which helps to code for the protein melanin.. This gene is normally active in cells called melanocytes which are found in the skin and eyes. Albinism involves a significant reduction or absence of the production of melanin, giving affected individuals a lack of normal coloration to their skin/eyes. Inheritance Pattern: normal melanin protein is produced by an autosomal dominant allele; albinism results from a lack of melanin and is caused by an autosomal recessive allele. Use the letter A or a to represent dominant/recessive forms of albinism. Two normally-pigmented parents have 3 children. The first child (a girl) and their second child (a boy) have normal pigmentation. Their third child (a girl) has albinism. That girl marries a normally pigmented male and they have four children. The first three (two girls and a boy) have normal pigmentation. Their fourth child (a girl) has albinism like her mother. *Draw your own Pedigree - Case Study #2: Condition of Interest: Huntington's Disease (also known as HD or Huntington's chorea) Huntington's disease is a neurodegenerative genetic disorder that affects muscle coordination and leads to cognitive decline and dementia. Inheritance Pattern: the allele for the normal "Huntingtin" protein is autosomal recessive; Huntington's disease is caused by an autosomal dominant allele which codes for an abnormal form of the "Huntingtin" protein. Symptoms are more severe in homozygous individuals. Use H or h to represent the alleles. A normal man (Joseph) marries a woman (Rebecca) who is heterozygous for HD and they have four children. Two of their sons (Adam and Charles) are born healthy without HD. Charles marries a woman without HD and they have a normal daughter. Joseph and Rebecca's daughter Tasha and their last son (James) both have HD. James marries a non-HD woman whose sister and parents also do not suffer from HD. James and his wife have three children - a normal boy, a normal girl, and a son with HD. *Draw Your Own Pedigree - Case Study#3: Trait: blood type Blood type is determined by the presence of several different proteins found on the surface of red blood cells. Blood type “A” has the A protein; blood type “B” has the B protein; blood type AB has both; blood type O has neither. The +/- indicates another protein called Rh. Forms of the trait: inheritance via autosomal multiple allelism (A, B, or O) results in the blood types A, B, AB or O. The alleles for blood protein A and B are codominant, the "O" allele is recessive to both the A and B alleles. Use AA, AO, AB, BB, BO or OO to represent the genotypes. As a 9th-grade school project, Maureen decides to trace the inheritance of blood types through her extended family, all the way back to her great-grandmother Katherine. Here’s what Maureen found out…. Maureen’s great-grandmother Katherine, has A type blood. Katherine and her husband John had four children – two sons, Michael (who has blood type AB) and David (who has type O blood); a daughter (Jessica) with type O blood and another daughter (Jennifer) with type A blood. Jessica never married; her sister Jennifer did get married and had three sons (one with type A blood, one with type AB blood and one with type O blood). Both of Katherine's sons also get married – Michael marries a woman with type O blood and together they have two daughters (Anna – type A; Leanne – type B); David marries a woman with type A blood, and they have three children (daughter Fran and son Albert who both have type A blood, and a son Matthew with type O blood). Matthew marries Janine and together they have one daughter, Maureen. Maureen knows that her parents both have the same blood type, but she has never yet had a blood test to determine her own blood type. Look carefully at the pedigree drawn below and match it to one of the choices given. Write your answer on the line provided. Most likely, the trait being tracked in this family is: a) autosomal recessive b) autosomal dominant c) X-sex linked recessive *EXTENSION: Draw Your Own Pedigree – Case Study #4 Condition of Interest: Hemophilia Hemophilia is a blood clotting disorder in which one of the proteins needed to form blood clots is missing or reduced (commonly, the protein known as Factor VIII). Individuals have difficulty forming blood clots following injury and may suffer significant blood loss from even minor cuts and bruises. Inheritance Pattern: Factor VIII is an essential blood clotting protein which is formed by a normal allele found on the X chromosome; hemophilia is caused by a lack of Factor VIII which results from a recessive allele found on the X chromosome. Remember that because this is an X-linked disorder, when you identify genotypes in this pedigree, you must use the XX/XY notation and use superscripts with each X chromosome to indicate whether the “H” (normal) or “h” (hemophilia) allele is present. (Ex. XHY = normal male) Hemophilia became known as the “Royal disease” after it suddenly cropped up in some of the descendents of Great Britain’s Queen Victoria and spread through the royal families of Europe. Queen Victoria and her husband Prince Albert had 9 children – 5 girls (Beatrice, Victoria, Alice, Helena, and Louise – none of whom were hemophiliacs) and 4 boys (Edward, Alfred and Arthur had normal blood clotting; their son Leopold, however was a hemophiliac). Beatrice married a man named Henry and they had four children (sons Leopold and Maurice who were hemophiliacs, daughter Eugenie who was not a hemophiliac, and another son who was also not a hemophiliac). Eugenie married Alfonso XIII of Spain (non-hemophiliac) and they had 6 children (2 normal sons, 2 normal daughters and 2 hemophiliac sons). M - Mutualism- a symbiotic relationship that benefits both organisms involved. C - Commensalism- a symbiotic relationship that benefits one organism and the other is not helped or harmed. P - Parasitism- a symbiotic relationship that benefits one organism and the other is harmed. ____ 1. A tick living on a dog. Symbiosis organism 1 organism 2 ____ 2. A tapeworm living in a 6th grade student’s intestines. Mutualism ____ 3. A bird building their nest in a tree. Commensalism ____ 4. The hermit crab carrying the sea anemone on its back. Parasitism ____ 5. A whale and barnacles. ____ 6. Head lice living on a human scalp. ____ 7. The ants protecting the acacia tree and tree provides food for the ants. ____ 8. Orchids growing in tall tropical trees, the trees are not harmed but the orchids get sunlight. ____ 9. A sixth grader and their pet. ____10. Algae growing on the fur of a sloth, giving it camouflage. ____11. Small mites live on your skin, eating dead skin cells. You don’t even notice. ____12. The clownfish and the sea anemone. 1. Oxpecker and zebras: Oxpeckers are a type of small bird that land on zebras and eat ticks and other parasites that live on the zebra’s skin. The oxpeckers get food and the zebras get pests removed. Organism 1: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Organism 2: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Symbiotic Relationship: _____________________________ 2. Tapeworm and animals: Tapeworms are segmented flatworms that attach themselves to the insides of the intestines of animals such as cows, pigs, and humans. Tapeworms get food by eating the host's (animal) partly digested food, depriving the host (animal) of nutrients. Organism 1: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Organism 2: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Symbiotic Relationship: _____________________________ 3. Spider crab and algae: Spider crabs live in shallow areas of the ocean floor, and greenish-brown algae lives on the crabs' backs, making the crabs blend in with their environment, and unnoticeable to predators. The algae get a good place to live, and the crab gets camouflage. Organism 1: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Organism 2: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Symbiotic Relationship: _____________________________ 4. Remora and the shark: Remora fish are small fish that make their niche by picking up the scraps that sharks leave behind while feeding. The shark makes no attempt to prey on the remora fish. Organism 1: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Organism 2: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Symbiotic Relationship: _____________________________ Name: _________________________________________________________Date: _________ 5. Bee and the flower: Bees fly from flower to flower-gathering nectar, which they make into food. When they land in a flower, the bees get some pollen on their hairy bodies, and when they land in the next flower, some of the pollen from the first one rubs off, pollinating the plant. Organism 1: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Organism 2: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Symbiotic Relationship: _____________________________ 6. Bacteria and the human colon: Bacteria live in the colon of humans and are able to feed off the indigestible food that the human body cannot break down (cellulose of plants). In the process of breaking down the food, the bacteria also make much-needed vitamins that the human body in turn can use to keep healthy. Organism 1: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Organism 2: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Symbiotic Relationship: _____________________________ 7. Dog and the tick: Ticks live on dogs and feed off the dog’s blood. They may also infect the dog with a parasite that can cause the dog to become quite sick. Dogs also are sometimes found to be very tired because a large volume of their blood has been drained. Organism 1: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Organism 2: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Symbiotic Relationship: _____________________________ 8. Ostriches and gazelles: They feed next to each other and watch for predators, alerting each other to danger. Since the visual abilities of the two species are different, they each can identify threats the other animal would not as readily see. Organism 1: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Organism 2: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Symbiotic Relationship: _____________________________ 9. Hermit crabs and snails: Hermit crabs live in shells made and abandoned by snails. Organism 1: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Organism 2: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Symbiotic Relationship: _____________________________ 10. Cuckoo and warbler: A cuckoo may lay its eggs in a warbler’s nest. The cuckoo’s young will displace the warbler’s young and will be raised by the warbler. Organism 1: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Organism 2: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Symbiotic Relationship: _____________________________ 11. Mistletoe and spruce tree: Mistletoe takes water and nutrients from the spruce, harming the tree. Organism 1: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Organism 2: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Symbiotic Relationship: _____________________________ 12. Honey guide birds and badgers: Honey guide birds alert and direct badgers to bee hives. The badgers then expose the hives and feed on the honey first. Then the honey guide birds eat. Organism 1: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Organism 2: helped harmed not harmed/not helped Symbiotic Relationship: _____________________________

uploads/science/Teacher sheet lesson eig.searchText: ﻿Teacher sheet lesson eight Introduction You have learned about diverging and converging plate boundaries. In this lesson you will summarise information about these boundaries and explore a third type, a transform boundary. What type of plate boundaries do volcanoes form at? Task 1 — Compare and contrast Student information: Complete the table that compares and contrasts different types of plate boundaries. Use the document ‘Comparison table for plate boundaries’ and complete using information and images from the internet and your notes and recordings. Teacher information: The table can be found in the following pages of this document. Task 2 — Movie Maker animations Student information: Use movie making software such as Movie Maker to make animations of the three types of plate boundaries compared in the table. The animations need to be labelled and show the landforms and events that result from plate movement. You will need to take still images of diagrams to create this animation. Submit your completed file to your teacher. Teacher information: You may need to familiarise the students with the movie making software they will be using. Comparison table for plate boundaries Converging Diverging Transform Insert a picture. In which direction are the plates moving? What landforms are created? What types of events are caused by the movement? Where are these boundaries on the planet? Insert two photos of these boundaries. How is each boundary similar? How is each boundary different?

uploads/science/Teacher sheet lesson one.searchText: Teacher sheet lesson one Introduction This unit will be organised around an edStudio presentation that will contain the majority of the student resources. All of the investigations will be listed in the find and prepare sections of the lesson plans. Each page of the edStudio will be a new lesson and the students can individually work through the activities and submit their produced work electronically back onto the pages via the digital drop boxes. The edStudio presented in this unit will need to be personalised for each individual class. You will need to make a copy of the edStudio and then alter the permissions and/or modify the content to suit specific classes. It is possible to teach the lessons without the edStudio. If you do not wish to use it, a full list of the resources used has been included in the lesson plans. Student instructions for activities, that appear as pop-up boxes in the studio, are included on each teacher sheet as student information. Introduction — The structure of the Earth (website) Student information: Welcome to the unit. Today we will be looking at a slideshow that revises what you learned about rocks in Year 8 and introduces the structure of the Earth. You will then be working in groups to build up a model of the Earth. Please follow the instructions on this page to work your way through lesson one. First watch the slideshow Structure of the Earth (http://media2. teachertube.com/files/articles/3933.ppt#256,1,Unit 17 STRUCTURE OF THE EARTH) Afterwards, your teacher will lead a discussion on what you have viewed. Task 1 — Introductory reading Student information: Open the website Structure of the Earth (http://scign.jpl.nasa.gov/learn/plate1.htm) and read the information about the layers of the Earth. Do not navigate away from this page. When you have finished reading, create a page of notes of the relevant summary points, then create a labelled scale drawing of the four layers of the Earth. You may complete this task in your science journal or you may create an electronic document and save it in a new folder for this unit. Teacher information: The Structure of the Earth website contains a few interconnecting pages. Ensure the students only summarise the information on the page that opens from the link. 1 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1 Task 2 — Make a model of the Earth Student information: Now you have read about the structure of the Earth you will construct a model. Collect your materials then follow the supplied instructions. Make a recording of your group building the model and submit it to your teacher. If you are unsure of how to record, read through the section ‘How to prepare a presentation’ below. Once you have finished, view another group’s recordings and models. Teacher information: Student instructions are provided at the end of this document. For this activity the students will need the handouts ‘Make a model of the Earth’ and ‘How to prepare a presentation’. Task 3 — From clay balls to the centre of the Earth Student information: In task two you constructed a model of the Earth from a description based on accepted scientific theory. How do we know what the Earth is composed of if we can never see all the layers? Use the activity From clay balls to the structure of the Earth to gain some ideas about how scientists are using experiments to discover what the inside of the Earth is made of. Teacher information: Refer to the website From clay balls to the structure of the Earth (http://geophysics.esci. keele.ac.uk/earthlearningidea/PDF/74_Clay_balls.pdf). A student activity sheet of the same title is included at the end of this document. You will need to personalise this activity to suit your class. Culminating activity — Discussion questions Student information: Think about the two activities that you have completed and then read through the discussion questions below and write your answers in your science journal. Consider other students’ answers and reflect on whether you agree or disagree. Discussion questions: 1. What did you predict the centre of the two plasticine balls was composed of? 2. Do you need to cut open the balls to make this prediction? 3. Would you need to open the balls in order to draw a definitive conclusion? 4. What is the difference between a prediction and a conclusion? 5. Have scientists made predictions about the Earth’s composition or drawn conclusions? 6. Will scientists ever be able to draw conclusions about the composition of the Earth? It is important for this resource that misconceptions are not created by the students engaging with the activity. Explain to the students that the activities they complete on the clay balls are not mini-experiments that mirror current scientific investigation. They are, however, investigating that it is possible to form hypotheses based on experimental evidence, which is how scientists are currently developing a concept of the structure of the Earth. 2 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1 Make a model of the Earth Materials: • Four colours of modelling clay • Plastic knife • Piece of paper for labels • Metric ruler • Four toothpicks Method: 1. You first need to be in groups of two or three and then collect your materials from the front of the room. Remember to organise the recording of your activity now. 2. Each group will be making one labelled model of a slice of the Earth. Use toothpicks and paper to make the labels. Below is an image of a finished product. Schoch, Catherine © The State of Queensland 3. This will be a scale model so the group will need to work out how thick each layer should be. You will be making a 1 cm:1000 km model. Look up the thickness of each layer in your notes from task one. You will need to include the inner core, outer core, mantle and continental crust as four separate layers (the oceanic crust will be impossibly thin on this model so use the continental crust thickness). Remember to record yourselves working out this information. 4. Once you have worked out the measurements for your model you may commence building it. Use a different colour of plasticine for each layer. You need to be careful that each layer is the correct thickness. One member of your team needs to narrate your procedure while you record building your model. 5. Once the model is completed you may make some little flags from toothpicks and paper. Label each layer with its name, size and composition. Don’t forget to keep recording. 6. Now hold up your model for the camera and give a short presentation on your finished model, including how and why you made construction decisions. 7. Your group is now finished this activity. Upload your recording to a computer and make some final editing adjustments before you submit the final presentation. 3 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1 How to prepare a presentation You will be completing several experiments during the course of your study this year. As part of these lessons you will be required to record your participation in and reflection on each one. We will be recording in an electronic format and keeping digital copies of these records. So, how do I do that? Good question. You will be provided with some form of recording equipment at the beginning of the lesson. This may consist of a camera, a video recorder or a digital voice recorder. You will use these items to make a recording of the experiment as your group is completing the activity. Remember, you cannot go back and record an experiment once your group has completed it. Things to consider Your presentation on your experiment will still need to have the elements of a normal experiment ‘write up’. So you will need to state in your presentation the following elements: • The aim of the experiment — what is your group trying to discover? • Your group’s initial hypothesis — what does your group think you are going to observe? • How your group is intending to investigate this hypothesis — this is an initial discussion of your method. • Images of your equipment during and after set up — name the equipment and say why it is the most suited to the task (e.g. because we are only using small measures of materials we will use test tubes instead of beakers). • A commentary of your experiment method including any safety considerations your group has recognised. • A commentary and any images of your observations — what did your group see during the experiment? • Your concluding statements, and a discussion of these questions: –– Why did you see your observations? –– Are they what you expected to see? –– Did you have observations that may have been caused by errors in your method? • Your group’s reflection on the experiment and an analysis of your level of success or failure: –– How did your group manage the experiment? –– How many errors did you think you made? –– How did your results compare with your hypothesis? In a written presentation you would normally write out descriptions of these points, but for an electronic presentation your group will need to speak about these aloud as the group is working through the experiment. It may be a good idea to nominate someone to act as the ‘presenter’ for the recording. They will be responsible for the main commentary and for asking questions of the other group members. Once the experiment is finished and cleaned away you can download your presentation and give it some finishing touches. If you are taking photos and recording your voices, then a slideshow may be the best option for your format. If you have a video recording, then some general editing and additional audio via a voice recorder may be a good idea. 4 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1 From clay balls to the structure of the Earth You made a scale model of the Earth for task two. How do we know that these predictions about the Earth’s composition are true? The Earth is very large and no one has been able to drill all the way to the core. This is impossible. For task three you will be looking at how scientists have come to formulate predictions on the composition of the Earth’s layers. Follow the steps below and conduct some tests on two objects to see if you can predict what the objects are composed of. Step one: Form into groups of two or three. Collect your materials from the front of the room. What are the two objects? Do they look the same? Do you think they are the same? Explain your answer. What do you think the inside of the objects look like? Note: You are not to cut the objects open during this activity. Make a list of the tests you could carry out on the two balls and then wait for the teacher to lead you in a discussion of your classmates’ ideas. Now take your two balls and complete some of the tests on them. Make a record of your observations for each investigation. 5 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1

uploads/science/Teacher sheet lesson sev.searchText: Teacher sheet lesson seven Introduction In the previous lesson you learned about formation of new crust at diverging plate boundaries. In this lesson you will examine destruction of old crust at converging plates. Task 1 — Convergent plate boundaries Student information: Go to the website Subduction zones (http://www.platetectonics.com/book/page_12.asp) and read about convergent plate boundaries. Open a new Word document, create a labelled diagram of a subduction zone and include events and landforms that occur in this zone. Save this in the folder for this unit. a) Why do volcanoes form at convergent plate boundaries? b) Why do some places seem to have lots of earthquakes? Task 2 — Subducting plate Student information: How do we know that one plate is sliding under another? Construct a model using the information provided in ‘Model instructions’. The model is based on data from earthquakes. Record your group’s activity and submit to your teacher. View another group’s recording. Teacher information: For more information about the subducting plate model, follow this link. http://www.geosociety.org/educate/LessonPlans/RealEvidence-SubductingPlate.pdf Reflection questions and instructions for this activity are included below. 1 of 3 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson7 Model instructions The model you will be making today draws on actual earthquake data to provide evidence for the existence of a subducting plate. Earthquakes occur deep inside the Earth and the depth and size of all earthquakes is continuously being recorded. Research the answers to the following questions to review your understanding of earthquakes. 1. What is an earthquake? 2. Where do earthquakes usually occur? 3. What is the difference between the epicentre and the focus of an earthquake? Form into groups of four. Follow the instructions below to construct a model that shows the shape of the Nazca plate subducting under the South American plate. Remember you will need to make a recording of the activity and save it in the folder for this unit. First you need to collect the following materials from the front of the room. • Box • Scissors • 22 balls (or beads) of three colours • Copy of the map (whichever your teacher has provided) • Copy of the earthquake data table • Glue • 22 paper clips • Masking tape • String • 2 rulers 1. Use the information in the table to plot the earthquakes on the map provided. 2. Lay the box on the side and glue the map onto the top-facing side of the box. The bottom of the map should face the open end of the box. 3. At each epicentre on the map punch a small hole. It only needs to be big enough for the string to fit through. 4. Each of the balls (beads) will represent the focus of the earthquake. Each focus was recorded at its particular depth and these depths are contained within the table. For each epicentre of the map, find its focus. You will then need to attach a ball to a length of string that matches the depth of the focus. Make sure that you use an appropriate scale or you will not see the pattern in your finished model. Start with the deepest earthquake so you know they will all fit. 5. Work through all 22 epicentres on the map and hang each ball at the depth of each focus. 6. When you are finished with your model, answer the following questions either in a Word document or verbally as part of your recorded presentation. 2 of 3 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson7 Questions 1. What information does an epicentre provide about an earthquake? 2. What is the difference between the focus and the epicentre of an earthquake? 3. What is happening to the rocks at the focus of an earthquake, and what do we call this? 4. What do you notice about the depth of the focus of the earthquakes as you go further inland from the coast of South America? 5. According to your model, what appears to be happening to the two plates that meet along the west coast of South America? 6. Draw and label a diagram of the model showing what is happening to the plates along the west coast of South America as described in question 5. 7. Describe the type of plate boundary that is present along the west coast of South America. 8. Explain how your data supports your conclusions in question 5. 9. How can your model explain the deep trench that lies off the coast of South America? 10. Use a map of the world that shows the plate boundaries to find some other areas where this same type of plate boundary is occurring. 11. How is volcanism related to this type of boundary? 3 of 3 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson7

uploads/science/Teacher sheet lesson two.searchText: Teacher sheet lesson two Introduction Student information: In this lesson you will be looking at the changes to the Australian continent. Our landscape has been formed through several geological occurrences. You will be working through two learning objects and collecting information from them in order to construct a timeline. This will need to be recorded in your science journal. Task 1 — The timeline task The timeline task is detailed in the document Snapshots in time which your teacher will give to you. You need to find photographs from the internet as learning object images cannot be copied. Work through the two activities on this page and gather evidence to include in your timeline. Use appropriate copyright and referencing practices. Teacher information: The activity Snapshots in time is found in the Queensland Studies Authority Assessment Bank. You will need to access this site and download a copy of this resource for students. In order to access the site you will need to register and receive a password. More information about this can be found on the teacher sheet QSA Assessment Bank. The activity includes a student booklet and teacher guidelines. The student booklet needs to be provided to students. A link has been provided in the lesson overview and lesson plan for the QSA Assessment Bank homepage. Task 2 — Learning object: Palaeotraveller Student information: Learning object one is called Palaeotraveller (https://learningplace.eq.edu.au/cx/resources/ items/2b7ec0d6-14e4-bb27-3fc0-30c4953efb14/3/viewIMS.jsp). It provides information relevant to various locations at different points in time. It also contains an animated world map so you can see Australia’s changing position during these time periods. Refer to the supplied instructions to guide you through this activity. Please do not spend more than 10 minutes on this activity. When working through this activity you need to think about: a) what changes have occurred to the Australian continent? b) what features of the present landscape give us clues? Teacher information: The learning object can be downloaded and saved into a common folder for the students to access. This may help with navigation speeds. A copy of the student instructions has been included with this document if you wish to use it as a handout. 1 of 4 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson2 Task 3 — Learning object: Travel back in time Student information: Use the learning object Travel back in time (https://learningplace.eq.edu.au/cx/resources/ items/5a902fa5-4e1c-13f1-e92a-60c19ffbf3be/7/viewIMS.jsp?.hb=true) and the supplied instructions to make notes about evidence being used to support geological predictions. Select some of these pieces of evidence to incorporate into your timeline. Remember you may need to find other images from the internet. Please do not spend more then 10 minutes on this activity. In your science journal, write a sentence on how you think scientists have used evidence to support geological predications. Teacher information: The learning object can be downloaded and saved into a common folder for the students to access. This may help with navigation speeds. A copy of the student instructions has been included with this document if you wish to use it as a handout. 2 of 4 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson2 Instructions for Palaeotraveller When you select the Palaeotraveller link, an introduction page will open up. You may click on the button to skip this. The home page will appear with a welcome message in the screen. Make sure the small window on the left of the screen reads ‘Cambrian’ (this is the earliest time period for this program) then press the go button. The screen will now load with information about this period in time. On the green screen will appear a map of Australia. The red outline is the current coastline of the continent; click on the button that says key in order to understand the different areas of the map. Open up a blank Word document and create a table using the following template. You will have more room if you change your page setup to landscape. Time period Position of Temp Sea level What What are Where is Description continent did the the main the green of life forms on planet continent changes cross? of Australia to the What look like coastline does the during this from the landscape period? previous look like period? here? Now work your way through several of the time periods, filling in the table with your information as you go. You will use this information to construct your timeline. Save your document to your personal folder or record in your science journal. 3 of 4 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson2 Instructions for Travel back in time Open the learning object and press the continue button at the bottom of the screen until you are asked to choose a collection. You will be given the opportunity to work through all four collections so it does not matter which one you choose first. Once you select a collection, four fossils will appear on the floating platforms. It will be your job to label them by researching the information on the website. Press the continue button. A time portal will open up on the screen. You can choose any of the fossils and drag them into the blue section of the time portal (the label will follow the fossil). You will then be shown a screen that has a Time Portal console at the top, then some instructions written in yellow and finally the fossil and label of the bottom of the screen. If you wish to enlarge the label, click on the cross on the top right. You can keep working with it enlarged. You will be given one piece of information on the label. You will need to use this to fill in the rest of the information. Each drop-down box will give you several choices. When you have found the correct organism, make the correct selections in the drop-down boxes. Then click on the picture of the organism and a picture should appear in the space on the right-hand side of the label. Your can then copy and paste the information on the organism into the white window on the label. It will expand to fit the information. Your label is finished now; press the button that says exit the time portal. This will take you back to the previous screen so you can select another fossil. 4 of 4 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson2

As a class, discuss the following questions: - - Why do some things float and some sink? - Why can an ocean liner float? - Why does a paper clip sink? Buoyancy (Floating) Whether an object floats or sinks is determined by the balance between the downward pull of gravity and the upward push of the water. This upward pushing force is called buoyancy. Pull of gravity Push of water Push of water Buoyancy (Floating) • If the downward pull of gravity and upward push of water are in balance, the object will float. • If the weight force down is larger than the upward push of the water on the object, then the object will sink. uploads/science/Testing for Nutrients.do.searchText: Testing for Nutrients There are some simple tests to determine the nutrients in food. You are going to carry out some of these tests, then test various food samples for nutrients Part A: Testing for sugars Equipment : 2 test tubes, labels, glucose solution, distilled water, Benedict’s solution, 250 mL beaker, Bunsen burner, tripod and gauze mat. Procedure : Label two test tubes (A and B) and place them in a test tube rack. Add 5 mL of glucose solution to test tube A. Add 5 mL of distilled water to test tube B. To each test tube, add 5 drops of Benedict’s Solution Place the two test tubes in a 250 mL beaker containing 150 mL of water. Place the beaker on a wire mat over a tripod and heat with a Bunsen burner. Bring the water to the boil and leave the test tubes in the water until a change occurs. Record your results below. Results: Contents of tube Observations Test tube A Glucose Test tube B Water Conclusion : Part B: Testing for fats Equipment : Brown paper, oil, water. Procedure : Label two pieces of brown paper A and B. Add two drops of oil to the centre of A. Add two drops of water the centre of B. Allow the paper to dry, then hold it up to the light. Lipids leave a transparent mark. Record you results below. Results : Substance on Paper Observations Paper A Oil Paper B Water Conclusion : Part C: Testing for Protein Equipment : 2 test tubes , labels, protein solution, distilled water, Sodium hydroxide solution, Copper sulphate solution Procedure : Label the test tubes A and B. Add 10 mL of protein solution to test tube A. Add 10 mL of distilled water to test tube B. To each tube, add 10 drops of sodium hydroxide solution. Tilt the test tube and add two or three drops of copper sulphate solution down the side of the tube. A violet ring at the surface indicates protein. Record your results below. Results : Contents of Tube Observations Test Tube A Protein Test Tube B Water Conclusion : Part D: Testing for starch Equipment : Two test tubes, labels, starch solution, distilled water, iodine solution. Procedure : Label the test tubes A and B. In tube A , put 10 mL of starch solution. In tube B, put 10 mL of distilled water. Add 3 drops of iodine solution to each tube. Iodine turns black in the presence of starch. Record your results below. Results : Contents of Tube Observations Test Tube A Starch Test Tube B Water Conclusions : Part E: Testing Foods Use the steps outlined in parts A to D to identify the presence of nutrients in different food samples. Record your results in the table below. Food Tested Sugar Fats Protein Starch Questions: Which food had the most different types of nutrients present? Which nutrients did it have? You can show these forces in a diagram such as Figure 7.1.5 by representing each as an arrow. The size of the arrow represents the size of the force, so the bigger the arrow, the bigger the force. Force A is the largest of these three forces and force C is the smallest. x A FIGURE 7.1.5 Forces are represented B by arrows that show the direction in which the force acts. \c Balanced forces The forces acting on an object can be balanced or unbalanced. When sitting on a chair, the force of gravity pulls you downwards, towards Earth. The chair supports you by pushing upwards. his balances the downwards furce of gravity. This balancing act is shown in Figure 7.1.6. 9 FIGURE 7.1.6 The downwards force of gravity is balanced by the upwards support force from the chair. The forces acting on this person are balanced. Balanced forces don’t always mean that the object is stopped—it might be travelling at the same speed without changing directions (Figure 7.1.7). Consider Nishika, about to ride her bike. To take off, Nishika must accelerate, pedalling quickly and hard to produce a force large enough to push her forwards. Another force is acting against her: friction. Forces of friction could slow her down, such as the roughness of the road and the air she pushes through. To speed up, Nishika keeps accelerating. Her pedalling needs to provide a driving force that is bigger than the force of friction acting in the opposite direction. As Nishika continues her journey, she may travel at a constant speed without slowing down or speeding up. When this happens, the driving force from her pedalling is cancelled out by the friction forces pushing her backwards. Balanced forces ‘The forces acting on an object can be balanced or unbalanced. When sitting on a chair, the force of gravity pulls you downwards, towards Earth. The chair supports you by pushing upwards. This balances the downwards force of gravity. This balancing act is shown in Figure 7.1.6. 9 FIGURE 7.1.6 The downwards force of gravity is balanced by the upwards support force from the chair. The forces acting on this person are balanced. Balanced forces don’t always mean that the object is stopped—it might be travelling at the same speed without changing directions (Figure 7.1.7). Consider Nishika, about to ride her bike. To take off, Nishika must accelerate, pedalling quickly and hard to produce a force large enough to push her forwards. Another force is acting against her: friction. uploads/science/The Blueprint of Life.do.searchText: The Blueprint of Life Every cell in your body has the same "blueprint" or the same DNA. Like the blueprints of a house tell the builders how to construct a house, the DNA "blueprint" tells the cell how to build the organism. Yet, how can a heart be so different from a brain if all the cells contain the same instructions? Although much work remains in genetics, it has become apparent that a cell has the ability to turn off most genes and only work with the genes necessary to do a job. To build the body, the code carried on messenger RNA travels to the ribosomes where three bases within the code (called a codon ) specify a single amino acid . A long mRNA chain could contain thousands of these amino acids. When linked together, the amino acids form proteins , which make up many structures in the body. In this section, colo u r the bases and RNA chain the same as you did previously. Colo u r the amino acids red. DNA Replication Each time a new cell is made, the cell must receive an exact copy of the parent cell DNA. The new cells then receive the instructions and information needed to function. The process of copying DNA is called replication . Replication occurs in a unique way – instead of copying a complete new strand of DNA, the process “saves” or conserves one of the original strand s . For this reason, replication is called semi-conservative . When the DNA is ready to copy, the molecule “unzips” itself and new nucleotides are added to each side. The image showing replication is similar to the DNA and mRNA colo u ring. Note the nucleotides are shown as 2 parts – the sugar and phosphate (colo u r blue) and one of the four bases identified by shape, colo u r the same as you did on the other model. uploads/science/The Cloud In The Bottle..searchText: ﻿The Cloud In The Bottle Overview Students are already interested in the weather and can be made increasingly aware of cloud formation by this rather simple in-class demonstration. Purpose The purpose to this activity is to demonstrate to the students the direct effects of pressure and temperature on cloud formation. Objectives 1. Students will view an illustration of the principles involved in cloud formation. 2. Students will apply these principles to weather maps to predict cloud formation and clearing. 3. Students will observe how nuclei are necessary for the attachment of condensation in order to form clouds. Resources/Materials 1. Wide mouth gallon pickle jar 2. Heavy duty clear plastic bag 3. Rubber bands or masking tape 4. Matches Activities and Procedures 1. Place about 20 ml of water in a wide mouth gallon pickle jar. 2. Place a lit match into the jar. 3. Quickly place a heavy duty clear plastic bag over the mouth of the jar and secure a firm seal by placing a rubber band/masking tape around the top of the jar. 4. Push the bag into the jar quickly, then pull the bag out. Observe! Tying it all Together This activity illustrates how humidity, temperature, and air pressure influence the formation of clouds. The water produces high humidity in the jar and the smoke introduced by the match provides nuclei on which the water vapor can condense. As the bag is pushed into the jar, the pressure and temperature in the jar increase, causing the jar to clear. Upon pulling the bag out, pressure and temperature decrease, allowing water vapor to condense and produce a "cloud" inside the jar. Questions For Further Inquiry 1. Why are smoke and water added to the jar? (They provide moisture and nuclei for cloud formation.) 2. What does pushing and pulling on the bag do to the jar? (They increase/decrease pressure.) 3. How would warming or cooling the jar affect the observations? (They decrease/increase cloud formation.) 4. Relate your findings to weather conditions necessary to produce cloudy/clear skies. For articles, maps, or other media pertaining to this topic, look up the following in Encarta® Encyclopedia: Cloud Meteorology Troposphere For additional online information and media, view the following Encarta articles: Cloud Meteorology Troposphere For additional relevant information, visit the following Web sites: Cloud Catalog http://covis.atmos.uiuc.edu/guide/clouds/html/cloud.home.html
