uploads/science/waves_science_year_9__gz.searchText: Waves and Rays What is light? Light is a form of energy that we can see and is given out by hot objects. It is made up of waves that travel outwards from a light source. Some of the waves reach our eyes, but most continue elsewhere. Waves can be transverse or longitudinal The two main types of waveform are transverse waves and longitudinal waves. All types of electromagnetic waves, including light, as well as water waves travel as transverse waves. Sound waves travel as longitudinal waves. Transverse waves (light) are a moving wave where each part of the wave travels up and down in repeating motion as the wave moves forward. These do not need a medium to travel through and can travel through empty space. Longitudinal waves (sound) are a compressing and expanding wave that needs a medium to travel in. A medium could be gas, solid or liquid. Sound travels as a longitudinal wave Sound waves are mechanical waves requiring particles. (a medium to travel through) Air particles vibrate back and forward creating repeating patterns of high (compressed particles) and low (spaced apart particles) pressure. One wave stretches from one compressed area of particles to the next. Waves of sound energy travel through air, water and solid substances. Waves transfer energy Waves are a means of transferring energy from one place to another without also transferring matter. Some waves need a medium (matter) to travel through in order to transport their energy from one location to another and are known as mechanical waves, such as ocean waves, sound waves and earthquake waves. Other waves can travel through the vacuum of space where there is little or no atoms. These are know as electromagnetic waves. Examples of those waves include light waves, microwaves and radio waves. 93 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Features of a wave Waves have troughs, the lowest point, and crests, the highest point. A wavelength is the distance between two closest crests. The amplitude of a wave is a measure of its height. The height is taken from a midpoint between a trough and a peak up to the top of a peak of a wave. Frequency of a wave The frequency of a wave is calculated by the number of waves that pass by a fixed point in a given amount of time. The frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). Because all electromagnetic radiation travels at the same speed then more waves of shorter wavelength will pass by a point over the same time as waves of longer wavelength. wave speed = wavelength x frequency Waves always travel at the same speed. A scientific value that always remains the same is called a constant. The constant for the speed of light is c = 3x108 m/sec or 300,000 kilometres per second. Because we know the speed of light, if we know either the wavelength (λ) in metres or the frequency (f ) in hertz then we can calculate the other. Wavelength = speed of light / frequency Frequency = speed of light / wavelength Light energy can travel as rays Light travels fast and in straight lines. At the speed of light, which is 300,000 kilometers per second, light from the sun takes about 8 minutes to travel 149 million kilometers to earth. Light can go around the earth 7 times in one second. Light travels straight, until something bends it. The straight paths of light are called light rays. 94 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Light energy can be reflected, refracted or dispersed Light travels in a straight line until it strikes an object or a force. Light can be: 1. Reflected by a mirror 2. Refracted by a lens 3. Absorbed by the object Light interacts with matter by transmission (including refraction) which is travelling through it, absorption where it enters but doesn’t leave again, or scattering (including reflection) where it bounces off. To see an object, light from that object— emitted by or scattered from it—must enter the eye. Transparent, Translucent and Opaque Shadows are created when light rays are stopped A shadow is a dark area that is formed due to light travelling in straight lines which opaque objects block. An object that stops direct light rays creates a shadow. The shape of the shadow resembles the shape of the object. The shadow created when the Moon blocks the light from the Sun to the Earth is called a solar eclipse. 95 | P a g e GZ Science Resources The length of the shadow depends on the angle of the light source The length of the shadow formed on the ground depends on the angle that the light rays hit the object blocking the light. If the light rays hit the object straight on, then this will create the smallest possible shadow. The greater the angle the light rays hit the longer the resulting shadow. The changing of length of shadow can be seen as the Sun moves across the sky. In the morning and afternoon, the shadows created are the longest as the Sun is at the greatest angle. The shortest shadows are formed at midday when the sun is directly over-head (in Summer). Sources of light and reflectors of light Light is a form of energy. The Sun is our most important source of light, which is produced along with heat energy, that is transformed from matter during a nuclear reaction. Other sources of light energy such as electrical lighting, fire and the glow from bioluminescent animals are produced during energy transformations as well. Light sources need energy to be transformed to produce light. These are also called illuminators. Objects that appear to produce light such as the Moon or shiny objects but do not use energy are reflectors of light. Light rays must originally come from a light source, such as the Sun’s light reflecting off the moon. 96 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Waves and Rays Review Questions 1. uploads/science/weathering and surface a.searchText: ﻿Chapter 8 Rocks extra worksheet 1: Weathering and surface area Science understanding Logical/Mathematical, Visual/Spatial Name: Class: Date: This worksheet is an extension of Pearson science 8 Activity Book Worksheet 8.3 Weathering experiment. This extension worksheet will help you to understand what happened in the experiment done by Sita and Glenn. To help you understand the results, you can model what is going on using an apple. Cut a piece of apple into a cube with 2 cm sides, as shown in Figure 8.1.1. Figure 8.1.1 Finding the surface area You can calculate or measure the total area of apple on the outside of this piece. There are six faces. The area of each face = 2 x 2 = 4 cm2. The total surface on the apple cube = 2 x 2 x 6 = 24 cm2. Finding the volume The volume of a cube is found by the formula volume = length x breadth x height The total volume of the cube of apple = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 cm3. Increasing the surface area Now cut the apple cube into eight cubes with 1 cm sides. Do this by cutting the cube in the middle of the length, the breadth and the height. Use Figure 8.1.2 to help you. Figure 8.1.2 The total volume of these 8 cubes is still 8cm3. So there is still the same amount of apple in them as in the single large cube. But there are now eight small cubes and each has six faces. Questions 1 Calculate the amount of surface now on one small cube. 2 Calculate the total surface of all 8 small cubes added together. 3 Compare the total surface of the 8 small cubes with the surface on the large cube. Now imagine the apple is like the marble rock that Sita and Glenn used in their experiment. The amount of surface exposed is important, because this is what the acid attacks first. The acid can only reach the inside by gradually removing the surface. If a big surface is exposed the acid can attack it all at once. So more rock is reacting with the acid all the time. 4 Explain how Worksheet 8.3 and this extension worksheet have helped you understand why physical weathering can help chemical weathering break down rocks.

uploads/science/What Are Minerals - Teac.searchText: What Are Minerals – Teacher Notes Minerals are natural materials which are: (1) inorganic (not created by living things); (2) have a consistent chemical composition; and (3) when solid have constant crystal structures. Inorganic Minerals are inorganic. What is the definition of inorganic? (hint: it doesn’t have anything to do with the ‘organic’ vegetables you can buy at the grocery.) Inorganic broadly means not created by or consisting of living matter. In chemistry, it also means something doesn’t contain the element carbon. Gallstones form in your gallbladder, which is part of your digestive system. Digestive fluid from the liver containing varying amounts of salt, cholesterol, calcium or bilirubin crystallises and makes rocks! These rocks can be as small as a grain of sand, or as large as a plum. They can block the bile outlet and cause pain. Most people do not know they have them until they start to feel pain. Are gallstones minerals? Explain your answer. No. The come from a living thing, and they have varying chemical composition Consistent Chemical Composition A mineral is made of the same combination of elements no matter when or where in the world it was formed. This combination of elements (or composition) is like the ingredients in a cake; every chocolate cake needs flour, water, eggs, and –of course – chocolate. The ratio (the amount of one thing compared to the amount of another thing) of ingredients is also very important; if you had 2kg of chocolate compared to 1 gram of flour, you wouldn’t have a cake! Similarly, every piece of quartz in the world contains silicon and oxygen in specific ratios. We write down the chemical composition in what are called mineral formula. In the table are some common minerals and their formulae. With the help of a periodic table, list the elements present in each mineral. Organelles are tiny structures within cells that perform specialized tasks and are often surrounded by their own membrane. These organelles perform the functions necessary to keep the cell alive. While there are many different types of cells making up an organism, most of these cells contain the same set of organelles: The cytoplasm is a viscous liquid that surrounds the organelles and acts as a site for many important chemical reactions to take place. The cell membrane is a semi-permeable film that holds the cell together, keeping the cytoplasm apart from the outside environment. The cell wall is a rigid exterior of plant cells, and is made primarily of cellulose. The nucleus holds all of the genetic information (DNA) of the cell in the form of protein recipes. Ribosomes are abundant, small production organelles that make proteins using DNA. The endoplasmic reticulum, a folded film sometimes studded with ribosomes, assists with the production and transport of proteins Golgi bodies package newly synthesized proteins for distribution out of the cell (secretion). Vacuoles are essentially membrane-enclosed compartments used for storage and regulation of internal pressure in plant cells. Vesicles are the storage organ found in animal cells. These tend to be much smaller then plant vacuoles. Mitochondria generate most of the cell’s ATP, the energy currency of life. Chloroplasts, only found in plant cells, are bright green because of the chlorophyll they use to generate sugar from light. uploads/science/Where Did the Universe C.searchText: Where Did the Universe Come From? Steady State Model . This is the old explanation. This says that the universe is infini te in size and has always existed the way it is today. Infinite means never ending. Big Bang Theory . This is a newer idea. It states that at one time in the past all of the matter in the universe was in one place. It then exploded (Big Bang) and all the matter started to spread out forming the universe. A man called Hubble worked out the Big Bang Theory. By studying light he noticed that the Galaxies in the universe were spreading out. He thought if they are all spreading out they must have all started in one place. Distance in Space In space because the distances are so far apart we have to use special units of measure. Light year. This is the distance light travels in one year. It is equal to 9.5 trillion km (9500000000000km). Try these Light Years (ly) To go from light year to Km multiply by 9500000000000. To go from Km to light years divide by 9500000000000 Km 1 9500000000000 2 28500000000000 0.05 Parse c. This is an even bigger unit of measure for distance. One parsec is close to 3 light years. Sometimes Mega parsecs are used.

uploads/science/Where Does a Star get it.originalPath: uploads/science/Where Does a Star get its Energy From.docx
uploads/science/Where Does a Star get it.searchText: Where Does a Star get its Energy From? The sun is a star. The stars you see in the night sky are suns. Our sun is just one of innumerable other suns. In a star 2 hydrogen atoms are joined together to make one helium atom. This happens over and over again, with many hydrogen atoms. When two atoms are fused together to make another element it is called nuclear fusion. When this fusion occurs a lot of energy is released. This is how a star gets its energy. The reason this can happen is because the sun is huge and has a lot of gravity. Gravity is the force of attraction between all matter. It is the gravity that causes enough pressure to “ squash ” (fuses) the hydrogen atoms together. In space we find Nebula. Nebulae are clouds of dust and gas. Slowly the dust and gas comes tog ether due to gravity. Eventually the cloud becomes very dense with a lot of gravity. This gravity gives enough pressure to cause the fusion. uploads/science/Wild Australasia.docx.searchText: Wild Australasia – Exploring the Natural History of Australia How was Australia formed? The supercontinent of Gondwana separated and Australia moved north. List and describe each type of landscape as shown in the video: Landscape Description Rainforests of Tasmania Australian Alps Northern Tropical Rainforests Eucalypt Forests River Systems and Billabongs Deserts Great Barrier Reef Shallow water, the largest living thing on earth. Formed during the last ice age, 10,000 years ago. What is a structural adaptation? Body part which helps an organism to survive in its environment. For example, strong claws or sharp teeth. What is a functional adaptation? The way an organism’s body functions which helps it to survive. For example, being immune to venom. What is a behavioural adaptation? The way an organism behaves which helps it to survive. For example, being nocturnal. Why are bushfires important to the Australian bush? Fire and smoke can help some seeds to germinate. Why are there more reptiles in the desert than mammals? Mammals are warm blooded and therefore require more energy. Ectothermic animals like reptiles do not require as much food, which is often scarce in the desert. What is the single biggest breeding event on Earth? Simultaneous release of eggs and sperm from the Great Barrier Reef. . uploads/science/WK- mixtures.doc.searchText: ﻿Chapter 7 Elements extra worksheet 2: Mixtures Science understanding Verbal/Linguistic, Visual/Spatial Name: Class: Date: A mixture of two substances can be divided into two components: • the dispersion medium, which makes up most of the mixture • the dispersed phase, which is the substance that is mixed into the dispersion medium. For example, when a teaspoon of sugar is dissolved into a cup of water, the water is the dispersion medium and the sugar is the dispersed phase. Both the dispersion medium and the dispersed phase can be a solid, liquid or gas. For example, when there is a dust storm, the dust is a solid dispersed phase and the air is a gaseous dispersion medium. Questions 1 Complete the following to identify the dispersion medium and dispersed phase for each mixture. Mixture Dispersion medium Dispersed phase a salt water b smoke from a fire c muddy water d fog e whipped cream The type of mixture depends on whether the dispersion medium and dispersed phase are solids, liquids or gases. The table below outlines the names given to various types of mixtures. Dispersion medium Dispersed phase solid liquid gas solid solid solution alloy (for metals) solid sol solution sol suspension solid areosol liquid solution gel liquid solution emulsion aerosol gas solid foam solution foam gas solution 2 Complete the table below to identify one example of each type of mixture. The first one has been done for you. What Makes the Electrons Flow? If you could see the atomic world inside a copper wire, you’d see that the atoms of copper can lose electrons so easily that there are billions of “loose electrons” hanging around between the atoms. These electrons are not going anywhere, but can easily jump from atom to atom. Copper atom Loose electron Every battery or other power source has an electric field. The field of a battery is produced by chemical reactions. The “mains” power is produced by magnetic effects in a generator at a power station. When the wire becomes part of a circuit, the electric field instantly reaches through the wire and exerts a force on every electric charge. The charged particles within the copper atoms cannot move, but the “loose” electrons immediately gain energy from the field and begin flowing in the wire. This flow of electrons is the electric current. The amount of “push” that the electric field can give the electrons is called “voltage”.
